The black-and-gold finish is sharp, the angled design is made for a comfortable fit, and touch controls handle music and calls. Battery life runs up to seven hours per charge and more than 30 with the case. They're water-resistant, too. A solid upgrade for the dad who still cares what comes through his headphones, even if he now listens at a more reasonable volume.

    It has been revealed that if he has opinions about beans, water temperature, and extraction times, he needs a grinder that can keep up. Fellow's Opus 2 handles everything from espresso to cold brew, with fine grind adjustments and 48-millimeter conical burrs. Anti-static technology cuts down on the mess, and magnetic catch cups make switching methods simple. The sleek profile doesn't hurt. But the point isn't the countertop aesthetic. It's better coffee before any guests start asking where their shoes are.

    This year’s Booker prize winner is a dystopian sci-fi satire that takes place up and down the British coast. It’s not exactly a beach read, but a novel that is a perfectly odd reflection of our perfectly strange times.

    Sources indicate that A slab of teak isn't an obvious gift until you see this one. Sonder LA's Bradbury board has three compartments for chopped ingredients or a serious cheese spread. Turn it over and a deep groove catches up to 4.5 ounces of carving juices, saving the counter from the aftermath of Sunday dinner. Heavy, handsome, and useful enough to leave out all the time. It's the cutting board version of buying one good thing instead of three mediocre ones.

    Smithey's cast-iron chef skillet looks like something a grandparent might have handed down, except this one comes ready to start its own history. The polished interior develops seasoning over time, the curved sides make tossing food easier, and the weight holds heat beautifully for searing. It's made in South Carolina and looks good enough to bring straight to the table. For the dad who finds chopping onions therapeutic and considers a well-seasoned pan a point of pride.

Made In's 8-inch chef knife is forged in Thiers, France, by a fifth-generation bladesmith, with a full-tang construction that gives it balance and control. It can mince herbs, chop vegetables, and tackle the Sunday roast without switching tools. The best part is how often he'll use it. Unlike most expensive kitchen gifts, this won't spend its life on display.

    Finding a night when everyone's free is now the hardest part of poker. Mark & Graham takes care of everything else: two decks of cards, 100 chips, and a pebbled-leather case lined in suede. It's compact enough to put away but handsome enough not to. Add a monogram if he likes that sort of thing. Then put an evening on the calendar and let him spend a few hours with people who don't need help finding their cleats.

The stainless-steel body looks good on a patio, and the setup is simple enough for an impromptu evening outside. Roast marshmallows with the kids or pull up chairs after bedtime. It's a small fire with an outsized ability to make an ordinary Tuesday feel like something else.

    Industry observers note that the mind of the famous neurologist Oliver Sacks was like no other. His letters show his thoughts in full light — restless, deep, and full of love and wisdom. Think of this book as competency porn — a counter to the daily doomscrolling.

    Chess is a wonderful game, provided you enjoy being intellectually humiliated by a 12-year-old. This smart chessboard might help him even the odds. Built-in sensors track every move, while LED lights suggest what to do next, and AI-powered coaching helps players improve without enduring another smug lecture about strategy. Connect it to Chess.com or Lichess to challenge opponents around the world, play against the computer, or settle a family rivalry the old-fashioned way.

    According to recent reports, A puffer jacket for your neck sounds ridiculous until the temperature drops. Cotopaxi's Fuego Down Scarf delivers the warmth of an insulated jacket in a lightweight, packable scarf, with responsibly sourced down, a water-resistant recycled nylon shell, and bold color-blocked stripes. A pull-through slit keeps it securely in place, while pockets at either end give Dad somewhere to warm his hands when gloves aren't enough.

    A leisurely hike is one thing. Scrambling up a rocky trail and navigating a steep descent is another. Leki's Makalu Cork Lite trekking poles give Dad some extra stability when the terrain gets tricky, without weighing him down. Made from lightweight aluminum, each pole weighs less than 9 ounces and has an ergonomic cork grip that absorbs moisture and gradually conforms to his hand. Adjustable locking mechanisms make it easy to change the length on the go, while carbide tips provide traction on uneven ground. They telescope down for packing, too.

    The nightstand looks like a cable graveyard. Anker's MagStand gives it a chance at redemption, charging three devices with a magnetic pad for compatible iPhones, a retractable USB-C cable, and another USB-C port. A small display reveals charging status and other information, while a quieter overnight mode suits a bedroom. It's the sort of unglamorous upgrade that feels extremely glamorous the first time he reaches for a fully charged phone and doesn't pull a nest of wires off the table.

    Sources indicate that for the Formula 1 dad with extremely confident opinions about tire strategy. Logitech's McLaren racing bundle pairs an F1-style wheel with direct-drive force feedback, so the steering pushes back as traction and cornering forces change in the game. It's far closer to a simulator than a standard controller, and requires the space and enthusiasm to match. A serious indulgence, yes. But probably less expensive than any other way of letting him pretend he's on the grid.

    Recent findings suggest that at some point in your parenting adventures, whether you like it or not, you will have to face the trials and tribulations of what it means to be a teenager. This book deeply, and sometimes even profoundly, explores just this, with equal parts science and storytelling, it might not help you truly prepare for your little one to hit their pubescence, but it will give you empathy and maybe even a bit of appreciation.

    Keys jangle, scratch phones, and vanish precisely when everyone is late. Orbitkey stacks three to seven of them inside a slim leather organizer, then adds a tracker that works with Apple Find My or Google Find Hub on compatible devices. It takes less room in a pocket and looks considerably better than a bulky ring. Not the showiest gift here. Possibly the one he'll use most often.

    It has been revealed that remember when listening to music meant putting on an album and actually listening to the whole thing? The Retradisc CD player brings back that pleasure, minus the tangled headphone cords. Its transparent case lets Dad watch his CDs spin, while Bluetooth connectivity lets him pair it with wireless headphones or speakers. There's also a traditional headphone jack, anti-skip protection, and a rechargeable battery.

    Industry observers note that some dads count steps. Others count elevation gain. Garmin's Enduro 4 is for the second group, with trail maps, endurance metrics, stamina tracking, and more than 100 activity profiles. Its solar-assisted battery can last up to 90 days in smartwatch mode under Garmin's specified sunlight conditions, which makes it especially useful on long trips. It's overkill for walking the dog. For someone planning his next ultramarathon before finishing the last one, that's the appeal.

    He tracks workouts, sleep, and maybe his resting heart rate. Why stop at weight? Withings' BodyScan 2 measures composition by body region, tracks muscle and fat mass, and offers cardiovascular metrics including a six-lead ECG and vascular age estimates. Results appear on a screen built into the handle. Some advanced analysis requires a subscription, and it's not a replacement for a doctor. Buy it for the data enthusiast who actually wants this information, not as a hint that somebody should get in shape.

    The fleece vest has spent far too long being associated with finance bros who say things like “let's circle back.” It's time to reclaim it. The North Face's Glacier Vest is lightweight, warm, and made entirely from recycled polyester fleece. It's the ideal extra layer for chilly morning walks, weekend hikes, or an office where someone has apparently mistaken the thermostat for a refrigerator dial.

    In a recent development, because exercise equipment has a way of proliferating and is generally ugly, at-home workouts tend to require a sacrifice of one kind or another. The possible lone exception is the rowing machine: Rowing works 86 percent of the body’s muscles and can be as cardio-intense (or mellow) as you like, while improving joint flexibility. One of the newest and sleekest rowing machines, the Ergatta uses actual water resistance, which makes it as effective as it is quiet (as well as cool-looking, with its transparent reservoir). It’s got all the fitness potential of a traditional rowing machine, but packaged with cutting-edge, immersive technology (a reasonable $29/month) that keeps monotony at bay.     Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. in Keratea, Greece, is a truly unique organization, at the moment home to over 100 cats and 13 dogs, living in a cage-free, home-like, villa-style environment. S.M.A.R.T. stands for Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today, and for Julie Kelley, founder and manager of this international animal welfare organization, that means working towards global animal welfare, sharing essential information and facts about animals worldwide, and helping people understand the benefits that come from treating animals with compassion and care.

    In a recent development, I had been traveling to Greece since 1998 and would see the challenges with stray cats and dogs. I felt very comfortable in Greece. I had business with Greek nationals in Latest York, learned a lot of the language, and understood the cultural differences. I felt it was my mission to create Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. to help people understand the great benefits animals provide to us humans and to educate young people as well. Of course, after a couple of years, it was hard not to take in the first kitty who gave birth, and well, it just grew exponentially from there! Since 2007, we have added many programs and special projects to continue our quest to provide the best we can for our strays.

    Letâs be S.M.A.R.T. aims to educate the public about the importance of animals by raising awareness of their rights, well-being, and care. We believe in thinking globally and acting locally by supporting special projects as they arise and, through our programs, bringing communities together to promote responsible animal care.

    Recent findings suggest that in Greece, our campaign is primarily centred on reducing the suffering, abuse, and neglect of animals while increasing public awareness of their needs and rights. These include running an innovative and modern foster home, managing a rehoming program for rescued animals, and collaborating with municipalities to implement effective stray animal care initiatives. We also provide practical solutions for supporting strays in urban communitiesâsuch as ensuring access to food and waterâand we actively engage philanthropic individuals who travel to Greece to volunteer, learn about shelter medicine, and receive training in best practices in animal care.

    It has been revealed that the creation of the sanctuary and setting up the organization in Greece was a huge accomplishment. Let's be S.M.A.R.T. is always evolving with fresh ideas to make life better for the cats and dogs we have in our care.

    Industry observers note that our campaign model is unique in Greece. We have created the âSMART Starfish approachâ in which all five arms must function together to create the best outcome.

    Each arm of the starfish represents a core pillar of our mission:.

    Sterilization â controlling population growth at its source.

    Medical Care & Microchipping â restoring health and identity.

    Feeding & Shelter â stability, nourishment, and safety.

    Education & Community â knowledge that shapes future behavior.

    NGO Collaboration â collective strength through partnership.

    For years, our programs and ideas have been influencing how animal charities operate and making permanent changes for a better future for animal welfare in Greece.

    Sources indicate that we created the following programs: Volunteer, SMART Family Video Series, Veterinary Internship, SMART Yards, and Adoption Vacation, all of which are operational every day and are detailed on the Programs page on our website, if you would like to take a closer look. We could not function without the help of our amazing Volunteers.

    We successfully found wonderful homes for 73 cats in 2025. I'm not 100% sure, but I would say we are one of the leading cat adopters in Greece!

    We receive multiple enquiries from tourists who have found a cat or kitten, and they want to take it home with them to their country. Many times they have cared for them during their stay, provided medicine, bottle-fed babies, etc. This has become increasingly common, with visitors seeing cats all over Greece. Therefore, I decided to offer the Adoption-Vacation as a package. We care for the kitten or cat until it is ready to travel, taking care of the necessary vaccines, passport, microchip, etc. Once the cat is ready to travel, we make travel arrangements with the adopter.

    You can see our cats, kittens, and dogs for adoption on our website and have a video chat with us about your requirements and meet a cat if you have already fallen in love (we created a Kitty Picker to help you choose the character of your cat), and then arrange a visit with us when you arrive in Greece. If the home check is secured, we arrange the papers for your new pet to travel home with you. Or we can foster a cat you rescue while you are in Greece and deal with the veterinary needs, papers etc. The cat can travel after you leave with a flight buddy or one of our volunteers.

    What better souvenir to have from Greece than a beautiful cat that needed special love and care?

    In a recent development, everything we do is linked. The more sterilizations we achieve, the safer and healthier the animals are in the community; they are interacting better with each other, and people know they are sterilized.

    We would like the municipalities and communities all over Greece to enjoy the benefits of the SMART Yards and help take care of the animals. Working together is the future. We are also collaborating with some officials regarding some policies involving the strays and to help create some standards for housing the strays. Animals and people need to coexist in a humane way. Not every cat needs to be inside a home but can remain cared for and part of our ecosystem.

    It has been revealed that A rather major goal is to find someone to help us purchase the property we rent, make refurbishments and sustainable features, and add a vet clinic for shared use with other charities and our vet interns. This is a tall order, but we are looking for someone who would like to leave a legacy.

    We also want to extend our ability to provide food and shelter after sterilization so that every animal is cared for.

    Recent findings suggest that our animals live in a home-style environment, so every day is the same as if they were living in a family home. Cats are either in bedrooms; we have a retirement room, a special dietary needs room, and a kitten nursery, each with cats that are selected to share a room together, or they are in the main house and free to mingle and hang out on our netted balconies in cute wooden houses and take in the fresh air and nature, since we are in a rural setting, just 15 minutes from Athens International Airport.

    According to recent reports, some of the funniest moments are with kittens and playful cats. Plus, bonded pairs â we have a husband-and-wife team called Jasper and Margot who need to be adopted together, and they are very entertaining with their games and spats.

    According to recent reports, cats and dogs choose who they like and want to go home with. We find people fall in love with cats that come to them, and a chemistry is formed. Sometimes a visitor leaves, and they cannot stop thinking about the cat they fell in love with and make an application to adopt. We are so happy when this happens. We have repeat adoptions from families and visitors all over the world. We also have Sponsors and Patreon for people to support our work.

    Volunteering is open to everyone around the world who would like to come to stay and help us. If you love animals, it's an opportunity to help save lives. It's pure joy to see a cat or dog that was sick transform into good health and finally live in a wonderful family home. That's what the team at Let's be S.M.A.R.T. wants for them all: to be safe, healthy, and happy.

    In a recent development, people can also help by following, subscribing, and sharing us on socials. Donations are greatly appreciated, as are supplies, and we created the Amazon Wishlist so gifts can be sent to us directly from Amazon Germany, tax-free.

    If youâre visiting Greece and see a lot of stray cats, itâs a good idea to ask around if there is a local organization helping to take care of them. If you see an injured cat, you should immediately try to find a responsible person or contact the local police.

    You can also post on local social media groups to try to find help. Most of the cats we take into our foster home settings are from tourists or residents who find our website through a Google search. It is hard to avoid helping, but I would suggest not removing an animal from their setting to a hotel room or Airbnb, and then leaving and putting it back on the street. The cat can get disoriented and perhaps be in danger.

    We truly hope to have more controlled community care for our strays in the future.

    In a recent development, this episode is sponsored by Pfizer. This article is directed to a U.S. audience and may not be suitable for those outside of the U.S. We partnered with them to bring you this conversation, but everything you hear from me, Chloe, and Dr. Chambers is our own experience and opinion. Not medical advice, just a conversation between moms.

    Pregnancy has a way of making you feel responsible for someone before you have ever met them. For actress Chloe Bridges and OBGYN Dr. Charis Chambers, that meant navigating the identity shift of newly introduced motherhood while also learning about respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a highly contagious respiratory virus that is the number one cause of hospitalization for babies in the United States with nearly 50% of RSV hospitalizations occurring during the first 3 months of life. Both moms built a trusted village of support to help navigate – and have a lot to say about what they wish they had known sooner.

    According to recent reports, in a candid conversation on The Motherly Podcast, Chloe and Dr. Chambers get real about the challenging transition into motherhood, learning to ask for (and accept) help, and what every expecting mom should know about helping protect their newborn from RSV infection.

    Sources indicate that chloe Bridges is an actress with a career spanning film and television. A Columbia University graduate, she welcomed her first child, her son Beau, with her husband, actor and comedian Adam Devine, in February 2024.

    Dr. Charis Chambers is a board-certified OBGYN and fellowship-trained pediatric and adolescent gynecologist known to millions online as The Period Doctor. She is the Chief Medical Officer at the cycle-tracking app Clue and the author of The Period and Puberty Parenting Revolution. She lives with her husband, Zachary, and their son, Joshua.

    According to recent reports, chloe: I think for me it was that everything is a phase. In the early days, I would get so nervous if something went wrong that day, you know, if he didn’t nap or wasn’t a good sleeper. I’d be like, ‘Oh my gosh, he’s never going to sleep. He’s always going to be a bad sleeper.’ And I just had to learn that a good day today doesn’t necessarily mean a good day tomorrow. A bad day today doesn’t mean a bad day tomorrow. Everything is just constantly changing and in flux.

    It has been revealed that dr. Chambers: The first lesson was really that I just can’t do it all by myself. I take pride in being able to accomplish things, and I am so proud of the things I have accomplished, professionally, personally. But motherhood is not one of those things where there’s a badge of honor when you suffer. So I had to learn, from the newborn phase to the late infancy phase to now, that I need help. Sometimes I need help because I can’t be in two places at once. Sometimes I need help because I don’t feel well. Sometimes I need help because I need to be restored, and I need a break. And all of those are really good reasons to ask for help.

    Sources indicate that chloe: I didn’t know what I didn’t know. It was almost like I didn’t want to think about postpartum too much, because I truly didn’t know what to expect. Everyone talks about how it’s just such a big transition, and I did really feel that. What’s that thing that people say? Two people are born that day. The baby is born, but then you are also born as a mother. And I absolutely experienced that. You can try to prepare mentally for what it’s going to feel like, but it’s still so surreal when it actually happens.

    Dr. Chambers: I immediately threw up my hands in thanks, and then I looked around like, ‘Wait a second.’ Everything is different. I felt like I didn’t even know which way to move or walk. I didn’t know what to do next. I just sat with that moment. My beliefs, my vision for tomorrow, my to-do list, it all just exploded, all in that moment. And it was immense joy, but a nervousness that I think is in proportion to just the depth and caliber of what this is.

    Sources indicate that dr. Chambers: As someone who spent so long not being a mother, I never thought that motherhood would ever fully define me, and I still don’t feel that way today. I also think when you desire something so much, it’s hard sometimes to verbalize that desire. So knowing that you’re stepping into this role, this space, that has never really been in your control to step into, but that door is opening. It was an identity shift, but like an identity shift I’d always hoped for but never had the power to change. Becoming a doctor, I knew that. I knew I was going to go to med school. Once I got that MD, I was going to be a doctor. But this is almost like it’s not an earned thing. It is given. I knew it was a forever shift, but spending so much time desiring to be in that role, and seeing that for myself and not knowing if it was going to happen, that was a real identity shift for me.

    Chloe: I think a lot of the decisions I was making were just about being so much more cognizant of my own health. Before pregnancy, I don’t know if I was necessarily the healthiest person, but you get pregnant and suddenly it’s not about you, it’s about you and your baby. And your health is intertwined obviously. So it was just a lot of decisions about, you know, obviously I’m going to follow all the advice. I’m going to limit my caffeine intake and I’m going to avoid foods that could give me listeria. And I’m going to, you know, take my prenatal. All of a sudden I was thinking about my health so much more, in a way I hadn’t been before.

    Sources indicate that dr. Chambers: So many of the decisions that I knew I had to make, it was almost like I had the answers to the test, just because I’m an OBGYN. But then I started to realize that what I really knew about pregnancy was related to a role that I wasn’t playing this time. I was the actual patient. I had a point in my pregnancy where my cervix was shorter, and they were measuring it, and wondering, are we going to need to do something more invasive, like a cerclage, or can we just do vaginal progesterone. And my very best friend, it was her bachelorette party, but it was in a remote area of Mexico, and I said, ‘How can I reconcile potentially delivering early in this extreme prematurity state that we would be looking at because I just want to be on this girls’ trip?’ I had to just sit with myself, ‘All right, what makes the most sense?’ Of course my friend was amazing and was like, ‘Girl, say less. No one’s going to feel bad. Take care of you and your baby.’ But it just was hard. You want to do so many things, but at the end of the day, you have to stand in your values and stand in your truths and trust that the people around you will be supportive of that.

    Sources indicate that dr. Chambers: This day and age, it is just hard, but it depends on the topic. When I was making my registry, for whatever reason, I just couldn’t start it. There’s a billion strollers. What do you mean there’s this many cribs? I was so overwhelmed. So I gave my sister my login and mentioned, ‘Go to town.’ But as it related to my health, being someone who had a high-risk pregnancy, it was a meeting of the minds. I made sure all of my doctors were on the same page, and I wanted a yes. Like when you’re in the emergency row of the flight and they’re like, ‘Yes, yes, yes.’ ‘Nephrologist?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘High-risk doctor?’ ‘Yes.’ OBGYN who’s doing the delivery, yes. I trusted my team.

    It has been revealed that chloe: I was also overwhelmed by the whole registry process. But I don’t have a lot of friends who have been pregnant before me, so I was leaning on the internet a lot. Dr. Google, and honestly lots of YouTube videos, all those videos of people being like, ‘This is what’s on my registry,’ or ‘Day in the life.’ And then my OBGYN was so helpful. I would be lost without her. She was truly such a resource, and I really felt like I had built a trust with her, and it really paid off later during birth and everything. I felt like I could ask her anything and trusted her advice.

    It has been revealed that dr. Chambers: RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, is a highly contagious respiratory infection that can get really serious for our youngest babies. When we think about the seasonality of it, it tends to run during the fall and winter months, and the seriousness is that it can lead to hospitalization. It can lead to infant mortality. This is a very serious thing.

    According to recent reports, dr. Chambers: Cold and flu can look like fevers and things of that nature. Sometimes it isn’t terribly respiratory leaning. But RSV has a lot to do with how your baby breathes, the retraction signs, and the work of breathing is the term that we use. Babies can get really, really exhausted and tired, and that noisy type of rapid breathing, those are all red flags that something is wrong. These are not all the possible symptoms of RSV in infants, so it’s important to talk to your doctor. If you notice any symptoms in your baby, talk to your baby’s doctor right away.

    It has been revealed that dr. Chambers: During those early months of life, that’s when your baby is at highest risk. Their immune systems are slowly building up, and when we’re thinking about the way RSV might affect an adult, it is not the same for your infant. So if it’s just vaguely on your radar, it’s key to know that this deserves more prioritization. It deserves more energy, more research. If eligible, pregnant women may have the power to help protect their babies by choosing to get vaccinated with ABRYSVO® (Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine), Pfizer’s respiratory syncytial virus vaccine that’s given during 32 through 36 weeks of pregnancy to help protect babies against RSV infection from birth through 6 months during September through January in most of the United States.

    To avoid the potential risk of preterm birth, ABRYSVO should be given during 32 through 36 weeks gestational age. The most common side effects in pregnant women are injection site pain, headaches, muscle pain, and nausea. Low birth weight and jaundice can also occur in infants. Please keep reading for full Important Safety Information at the end.

    Dr. Chambers: Many moms don’t realize that they are constantly making antibodies to things they’re exposed to and passing those antibodies onto their babies naturally. The RSV vaccination uses that natural process by allowing the mom to create antibodies to RSV and pass them down to her baby. When you get the maternal RSV vaccine, you are helping to protect your baby from the moment they take their first breath. Maternal immunization is an important part of my prenatal care discussions because babies are at highest risk of infection from RSV during their first three months of life.

    Recent findings suggest that chloe: RSV wasn’t on my radar. It was something that I learned about from my OBGYN. She recommended I get ABRYSVO for it, and I remain very happy that I listened to my OBGYN’s recommendation to get ABRYSVO when I was pregnant, and that helped protect him during his first six months of life when he is so vulnerable.

    ABRYSVO should not be given to anyone with a history of severe allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis) to any of its components.     Important Safety Information & Use.

    Ask your healthcare provider about the risks and benefits of ABRYSVO. Only a healthcare provider can decide if ABRYSVO is right for you. Always talk to your healthcare provider about any side effects you may experience.

    You are encouraged to report side effects of vaccines to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Visit http://www.vaers.hhs.gov or call 1-800-822-7967.

    Industry observers note that individuals who received ABRYSVO during pregnancy are encouraged to enroll in a pregnancy exposure registry at 1-800-616-3791. The registry will monitor pregnancy outcomes.

    ABRYSVO is a vaccine indicated for pregnant individuals at 32 through 36 weeks gestational age for the prevention of lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) and severe LRTD caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in infants from birth through six months of age.

    Please see full Prescribing Information for ABRYSVO at pfi.sr/ABRYSVO_PI.

Whether you're a latest pet parent or a seasoned cat lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions.     My 1-year-old cat Daisy has allergies. She is on a special hydrolyzed diet. Iâm trying to find an allergen-neutralizing spray to cut back on dust mites in the house. Would you recommend any specific products?

    Since Daisy is already on a hydrolyzed diet, it makes sense to look at environmental allergens too, especially if her allergic signs are continuing. Dust mites are common household allergens, and while the goal is to reduce the amount of allergens in her environment, eliminating them completely is not realistic. Regularly washing bedding and blankets, vacuuming with a HEPA filter, and keeping dust to a minimum are still the best places to start.

    If you would like to try a spray, Purefy Anti-Allergen Spray works differently from an insecticide. It is intended to neutralize or remove the allergenic proteins associated with dust mite debris, particularly the proteins found in their feces and other microscopic particles that accumulate in household dust and fabrics. Those proteins, rather than the living mite itself, are an important source of the allergic reaction. So the idea is not to kill every mite in the house, but to reduce the allergen they leave behind.

    I would specifically avoid routinely using insecticide or acaricide sprays around Daisy, even when a product is marketed as ânatural.â Cats can be particularly sensitive to certain botanical ingredients and insecticides, including some essential oils and pyrethroids. If you use an anti-allergen spray, follow the label carefully, keep Daisy away from treated surfaces until they are completely dry, ventilate the area well, and never spray it directly on her or on surfaces she is likely to lick. Please ensure you also keep it away from food and water bowls.

    Think of the spray as an extra layer of environmental control, not a treatment for Daisy's allergy. The unglamorous combination of washing, HEPA vacuuming, and reducing dust is still doing most of the heavy lifting. And if Daisy continues to have significant allergic signs despite a properly conducted hydrolyzed diet trial and environmental management, it is worth investigating other possible triggers rather than simply reaching for stronger household chemicals. Usually, the answer is not a more powerful spray, but figuring out exactly what is making your cat itchy. So, real detective work is often needed for success.

    Some kittens steal your heart with their big eyes. Others win you over with their playful antics. And then there's Gelato, a tiny kitten who needed a wheelchair and ended up getting one made from Hot Wheels cars. Yes, really. Human ingenuity and humane creativity to the rescue!

    Becoming more mobile in a Hot Wheels wheelchair might seem like a dream come true, but today, Gelato has even more reasons to celebrate: Heâs found his forever home.

    Gelato arrived at Cincinnati Animal CARE in Ohio as a stray kitten with a lower-back injury that left him unable to use his hind legs normally. The shelter team wanted to help him move around, but there was a rather inconvenient problem. The wheelchairs they had available were too major for his tiny body.

    Now, anyone who has lived with a kitten knows that, besides being irresistibly cute, they can be remarkably determined little creatures. They want to explore everything, investigate every corner, and get involved in whatever their humans are doing. Being unable to move around easily can limit those everyday experiences for the tiny fur balls.

    Fortunately, Gelato had people in his corner who weren't about to let his small size stop him from exploring the big world.

    The shelter's lead veterinary technician, Mallory Smith, came up with a wonderfully resourceful solution. She built a miniature wheelchair using cardboard, tape, zip ties, wooden rulers, and Hot Wheels toy cars. The first version needed adjustments, but Mallory kept working until the little device was ready to support Gelato as he moved around. While this is certainly quite a unique solution, what isnât unusual is the compassion and creativity behind it. Gelatoâs improvised mobility device is a perfect example of how animal medical care personnel go above and beyond to help patients in need.

    Recent findings suggest that gelato's homemade wheelchair was a clever solution to an immediate problem. However, a makeshift device is not necessarily the best long-term option for a growing kitten with mobility challenges.

    In a recent development, help arrived in the form of an engineer who created a custom 3D-printed wheelchair designed to fit his body and accommodate his growth. The toy cars were gone, but Gelatoâs future mobility was looking more stable.

    Gelato got lucky the moment someone refused to give up and asked, "How can we make this work?" This first lucky chance opened him to latest opportunities from a wider effort to help one small animal have a better chance at life. Itâs impressive how sometimes sharing an animal's story can make all the difference. A social media post can connect shelters with people who have the skills, resources, or homes that animals need.

    According to recent reports, giving Gelato a way to move around was an notable first step. And there was another milestone waiting for him: a loving family of his own.

    As the story of Gelatoâs unusual mode of transport spread, drawing plenty of social media attention, it also caught the eye of Hope Hollandsworth, a 28-year-old tattoo artist and devoted cat parent. When she first saw a photograph of Gelato during the summer, she felt immediately drawn to him.

    Hollandsworth already cared for two cats with spinal injuries, Bread Crumb and Sprinkles. Both have limited use of their hind legs and rely on their front legs for mobility. She understood that caring for cats with special needs could involve extra responsibilities, adjustments, and plenty of patience.

    In other words, she wasn't going into this adoption without knowing that life with a disabled cat can look a little different. Cat lovers are abundant, but those experienced in caring for disabled felines? Not quite as plentiful.

    Hope wasted no time, adopting Gelato as soon as she met him at the shelter. The five-month-old kitten spent his first night in his latest home sleeping in her arms.

    Sources indicate that absolutely. A disability does not automatically mean that a cat has a poor quality of life. Cats with mobility challenges can still enjoy affection, play, exploration, food puzzles, comfortable naps, and the company of people they trust.

    What really matters is understanding the individual cat's needs and making reasonable adjustments to help them live comfortably.

    According to recent reports, for a cat with a spinal injury, this may include providing easy access to food, water, resting areas, and litter boxes. Non-slip flooring, ramps, and thoughtfully arranged furniture can also help some cats move around more safely. Depending on the injury, a cat may need help with bladder or bowel function, regular skin checks, or a rehabilitation proposal.

    These are not small details. Some cats with spinal injuries cannot empty their bladders normally, which can lead to serious complications without very devoted care. A veterinarian can assess bladder function, mobility, sensation, and other concerns, then explain what support the cat will need at home. The real challenge is finding someone with the time and patience to take over these responsibilities on a daily basis.

    Hollandsworth's experience with Bread Crumb and Sprinkles gave her a head start.

    In a recent development, gelato will continue receiving therapy in the hope that he may regain some use of his hind legs, but for now, his recovery is uncertain. Spinal injuries vary, and a cat's prognosis depends on several factors, including the extent of the damage and the neurological function that remains.

    Industry observers note that but Gelato doesn't need a guaranteed recovery to deserve a happy future. He's got somewhere to go, someone to cuddle, and absolutely no need to prove that he can walk to earn his place in the family.

    His new family is ready to love and support him, whether or not he ever walks on his own. Hollandsworth put it beautifully: to her, Gelato is already perfect just the way he is.

    Sources indicate that there is a lot of wisdom in that simple sentiment. We can hope for progress, celebrate small improvements, and pursue appropriate treatment without making an animal's worth depend on how much they recover. Loving others, whether animals, people, or even ourselves, for who they are, exactly as they are, is what we call true love.

    #159219. Diagnosing a Ghost – The Mysterious Feline Disease Whose Signs Appear & Disappear

    📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1362 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Catster ↗ Open Full Page

    Diagnosing a Ghost – The Mysterious Feline Disease Whose Signs Appear & Disappear

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Catster

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you.
    • Industry observers note that waxing and waning signs, vague symptoms that come and go.
    • Recent findings suggest that in an autoimmune disease, a catâs immune system malfunctions and begins attacking the body it is meant to protect.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

    Industry observers note that waxing and waning signs, vague symptoms that come and go. A cat that is on deathâs door one moment, running around the next. Detecting illness in cats can be difficult enough, but when the body starts attacking itself, diagnosis becomes even more of a challenge.

    Recent findings suggest that in an autoimmune disease, a catâs immune system malfunctions and begins attacking the body it is meant to protect. Fortunately, autoimmune disease is relatively uncommon in cats, but it can be serious and difficult to diagnose and treat. Because the signs tend to be vague and can come and go, they are easy to overlook, which makes it worth knowing what to watch for and when to involve a vet.

    Industry observers note that A healthy immune system protects the body from germs such as viruses and bacteria by sending out specialized cells to locate and destroy them. It also helps clear away damaged or diseased cells. These immune cells use protein signals on the surface of the bodyâs own cells to recognize them as safe. In autoimmune disease, a signaling error causes the immune system to treat the catâs own cells as a threat, and healthy, working tissue gets attacked and destroyed.

    According to recent reports, cats can develop these problems much as people do. They can affect any part of the body, including the internal organs, blood, and skin, and there are many different types. Some can be life-threatening, weakening the bodyâs natural defenses while also damaging healthy tissue.

    The part of the body under attack determines which signs appear, so the picture varies dramatically from one cat to the next. Signs are often general and not immediately linked to an autoimmune problem. Possible signs include lethargy, weakness, decreased appetite, weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, and other changes to the feces. Other signs include pale gums, unexplained bleeding, bruising, a high temperature, a faster heart rate, rapid breathing, and tiring easily during play. Limping, swollen joints, sores on the skin, a poor coat, increased thirst, increased urination, and collapse are also on the list.

    Many of these signs come and go. A cat may seem completely fine one day and be struggling the next. Any of these signs are a reason to contact a vet promptly, since starting investigations early makes a real difference.

    According to recent reports, the problem starts with the catâs own immune system, which is part of what makes it so hard to manage. The exact triggers are not fully understood, and more research is needed. An immune-mediated condition can be triggered when the immune system is stimulated. Viral infections, vaccination, medications, inherited conditions, and hormones have all been linked to autoimmune disease. Where things get tricky is that the incident that triggered the disease is not usually the cause of the disease. That means that the same type of autoimmune disease can be triggered by different things in different individuals.

    Sources indicate that some of these conditions can be passed down, and other possible contributors include poor nutrition, toxins, cancer, and stress. A cat diagnosed with an autoimmune disease considered hereditary should not be bred under any circumstances.

    Diagnosis is often a process of elimination. More common causes of the same signs are investigated and ruled out first, which can mean lots of tests. A vet will start with a full physical exam and a detailed history, then choose tests to fit the signs. These may include blood and urine tests, X-rays, or an ultrasound scan. Samples may also be taken from wounds, rashes, or other affected areas. Prompt diagnosis is vital for effective management.

    Treatment depends on the type of autoimmune disease, what part of the body is affected, and what is behind it, so it varies greatly. The usual approach is medication that calms the immune system so it stops attacking the body, most often corticosteroids like prednisone or dexamethasone. A large starting dose is often given, and once the signs settle down, the dose is lowered gradually.

    Sometimes, stronger immunosuppressive drugs are also used. Some of them are also used in cancer treatment, and the side effects tend to be more severe. The trouble with treating an immune-mediated disease is that we are using medication to suppress the immune system, and that leaves the patient more susceptible to infection and other diseases.

    Even more challenging when treating feline autoimmune disease is that some of the medications used to treat dogs or humans are toxic to cats.

    Supportive care matters just as much. Pain relief is often needed, but many commonly prescribed anti-inflammatory painkillers cannot be given alongside steroids. Stronger painkillers like opioids or gabapentin may be used to manage severe pain, and these come with their own side effects. Antibiotics may also be prescribed, either prophylactically if extremely high doses of immunosuppressive medications are being used, or if secondary infections develop.

    For cats with immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA), where the immune system is attacking and destroying red blood cells, or immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (IMTP) where platelets are being destroyed, blood or plasma transfusions may be needed to save a catâs life.

    According to recent reports, lifestyle changes can help too. A cat with painful, swollen joints, for example, benefits from losing weight if overweight, and lower sides on litter trays and softer beds make life more comfortable. Each case is assessed individually.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the more common autoimmune diseases in cats is known as Eosinophilic Granuloma Complex, a group of idiopathic conditions that are presently quite poorly understood. The exact cause of the disease is unknown; however, parasites, allergies, and genetic factors have been identified as likely triggers.

    There are three main clinical presentations of eosinophilic granuloma complex:.

    It has been revealed that ulcerative: Also known as indolent ulcers or rodent ulcers, this form of eosinophilic granuloma complex usually presents with a sore on the cat's mouth. It is typically seen on the upper lip. They are normally red in color and do not appear to cause your cat any pain or irritation.

    Plaque-forming: often found on the stomach and on the inside of the hind legs. The lesions are often itchy and red and often become infected, which complicates matters.

    Granuloma forming: usually presents as raised pink or yellow nodules that can be located anywhere on your cat.

    Another more common feline immune-mediated disease is called pemphigus foliaceus. It affects the skin, causing scabs, crusts, and sores around the eyes and ears, on the paws, and in the groin area. When it develops on the paws, the nail beds can be affected as well.

    In a recent development, there is no cure for autoimmune disease, but effective treatment and management can control the signs, greatly improve quality of life, and allow most cats to live fairly comfortably. These conditions can be debilitating and life-threatening, yet it is often possible to manage them well enough for cats to lead relatively normal lives. Because the signs overlap with so many other conditions, a vet visit at the first sign that something is wrong is the surest way to get answers early.

    In Loving Memory of Tiger

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Catster

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

    This article is part two of From Misfortune to Blessing: How a Cat Lost a Leg, But Got a Forever Home.

    Tiger came to my family on 2 June 2025 after an accident at a car park that resulted in his right hind leg being amputated. Before surgery, he was diagnosed with Stage B2 Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) â subclinical heart disease with a high risk of progression. We were advised to follow up on Tigerâs heart condition.

    Having incurred a high bill for his condition in 2025, we brought Tiger to a general practice vet in Singapore, not a cardiologist. It was our first time rescuing a cat, and we didnât know the difference. The vet was more concerned about Tigerâs kidneys, and during several visits in 2025, she focused on his renal function. At each visit, she would listen to Tigerâs heart with a stethoscope and tell us the condition âshould still be the sameâ. Unknown to us, Tigerâs heart condition was quietly deteriorating.

    It has been revealed that in late December 2025, we suggested to the general vet that we book an echocardiogram to scan Tigerâs heart. We had to wait for the appointment, and it finally took place on 14 February 2026.

    When Tiger came home from the echocardiogram, he was extremely weak. He had not eaten since midnight the previous day; the gabapentin used to relax him for the scan made him so weak that he could barely stand up, and he pooped on the floor.

    The echocardiogram results took more than three weeks, and by then we were informed that Tigerâs heart condition had progressed from HCM stage B2 to congestive heart failure. Our vet asked for a one-minute video of Tigerâs breathing and told us his respiration rate was between 42 and 56, significantly higher than the normal upper limit of 30.

    Sources indicate that two days later, Tiger had a thoracentesis procedure at our regular vet to remove excess fluid from around his lungs, and was discharged a few hours later. He was also placed on furosemide (a diuretic) and clopidogrel (a blood thinner).

    Sources indicate that it was our first time administering medicine to a cat. Despite our inexperience, we managed to administer furosemide as it was a liquid. Clopidogrel proved much harder to administer; we tried hiding the tablets inside a pill pocket, but Tiger hardly ate it.

    In the initial few days after the thoracentesis procedure, Tigerâs breathing was less laboured. But I noticed that despite giving Tiger furosemide, he did not drink more water or urinate more often, and it didnât take long for fluid to accumulate in his lungs again.

    On 25 March 2026, Tiger had his first major episode of congestive heart failure.

    Recent findings suggest that he groaned and lay on the floor; his breathing was laboured, and he was experiencing nystagmus (involuntary rhythmic movement of his eyeballs). We immediately took him to the emergency room at Beecroft Hospital.

    In a recent development, at Beecroft Hospital, we were told that Tiger was about to âfall off the cliffâ and almost had a stroke. He had another thoracentesis procedure to remove fluid from his lungs and was placed in an oxygen chamber for observation for the next few days. We were told that the dosage prescribed by our regular vet was insufficient to control Tigerâs heart condition.

    After a few days, Tiger was discharged on the maximum dose of furosemide, together with a combination of other medications (spironolactone, pimobendan, rivaroxaban, and a potassium supplement).

    It has been revealed that the hospital nurse demonstrated the proper ways to administer Tigerâs medicine, which our regular vet had not done. Initially, we dissolved the pills in a small amount of water and syringe-fed him, but this method was messy and wasted some of the medicine. Later, we placed the different medications in a single capsule and used a pill popper to administer them. This proved much more effective.

    In a recent development, we had to feed the medicine at the same time each day, as delaying the diuretic by a few hours could cause the fluids to build up again. We had to adjust our life schedule around Tigerâs medication. We were also introduced to the Cardalis app to monitor Tigerâs resting respiratory rate.

    After being discharged from the hospital, Tigerâs breathing was normal at first, but within a week, we were back in the emergency room. This time his diuretic was changed to torsemide, a stronger diuretic.

    All in all, Tiger was in and out of the emergency room every week for a total of four visits, and the bills were mounting fast.

    Industry observers note that the cardiologist told us Tigerâs prognosis was poor and suggested euthanasia. We consulted an animal communicator who told us Tiger wanted to fight on. We were prepared for palliative care. February to April was a sad and emotionally draining period for us all.

    Industry observers note that with the stronger diuretic, his breathing rate was normal from May to July. We also gradually reintroduced his renal diet. It was a happy three months for us with many fond memories. He even bonded with my other cat during this time. For a while, we were able to forget about his palliative condition.

    Sources indicate that in early August, his breathing became laboured again, and he refused to eat his renal food, and I knew his kidneys would deteriorate fast on a normal diet. In the next two weeks, his appetite dropped, he hid more frequently around the house, and became increasingly lethargic.

    Sources indicate that from 20 August 2026 (Thursday) onwards, he would barely manage more than a few licks a day, and his weight dropped a lot. We could feel his spine and rib cage! He had not urinated for more than 24 hours, and we were so worried that his kidneys had totally shut down.

    On Friday, miraculously, he urinated a few times and had some licks of food. His last meal was on Saturday night.

    Tiger passed away naturally and peacefully at home on Sunday, 23 August 2026. He was so weak and lethargic, with barely any energy left, but still managed to get inside his little box and slept there. In this final moment, my sister calmed him to his final breath, and we were fortunate to witness his final, peaceful passing.

    Throughout this ordeal, Tiger was very, very resilient and wanted to live, but he did not get the chance.

    We held a private cremation for him on 24 August 2026, complete with Taoist chanting to guide him on his way. His ashes are stored at Mandai Pet Sanctuary in Singapore.

    Despite the financial, emotional, and time sacrifices, it was an honour to take care of Tiger in the final stage of his life.

    Now the room feels so empty in his absence.

    All that is left are loving memories.

    Sheryl Sin is an editor, proofreader, indexer and writer based in Singapore. Outside her work, she is a committed community cat feeder who takes care of the street cats in her neighbourhood. She is also mum to Cow Girl (an FIV+ black-and-white domestic shorthair adopted off the street) and Tiger (the tripod cat with kidney and heart challenges). Follow their journey on Instagram @sinmp24.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

    Cats come in all shapes and sizes. Some have legs that seem a little too long for their bodies, others have ears significant enough to pick up satellite signals, and a few look like they haven't quite grown into themselves yet.

    Usually, that's just part of the charm.

    Recent findings suggest that but when Gary and Shaggy were kittens, their disproportionately long limbs turned out to be more than an unusual-looking but perfectly charming physical trait. The two brothers would eventually become the first domestic cats confirmed to have Marfan syndrome through genetic testing; not exactly what any cat owner would expect when bringing home a pair of kittens.

    Recent findings suggest that as the cats grew, veterinarians identified abnormalities affecting their eyes and enlargement of the aorta, the major blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Researchers at Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine and the Baker Institute for Animal Health worked with veterinary and genetic specialists to investigate what was going on.

    Recent findings suggest that their long limbs were one clue. The eye abnormalities and enlarged aortas added two more. Slowly, the pieces of the puzzle began to fit together, pointing researchers toward Marfan syndrome, a rare inherited disorder far better known in human medicine than in veterinary practice. Genetic testing confirmed the connection, uncovering what made these two brothers so unusual.

    Sources indicate that marfan syndrome affects connective tissue, the body's natural support system. This tissue helps give structure and strength to the bones, ligaments, skin, eyes, and blood vessels. When something goes wrong with this system, the effects can show up in several different ways.

    In humans, the condition often causes unusually long limbs and fingers, a tall, slender build, eye abnormalities, and potentially serious cardiovascular complications.

    Abraham Lincoln was famously tall and lanky, which has led to speculation that he may have had Marfan syndrome. No one can say for sure, though. Turns out, even Honest Abe left a few medical mysteries behind!

    Recent findings suggest that for Olympic volleyball player Flo Hyman, long limbs gave her an edge on the court. However, her life was tragically cut short, dying at age 31 from cardiac complications from Marfan syndrome.

    One of the genes involved in Marfan syndrome is called FBN1. It contains the instructions for producing fibrillin-1, a protein that helps maintain the structure and function of connective tissues throughout the body.

    When that gene doesn't work as it should, the effects can extend well beyond a person's or animal's appearance. As the gorgeous ginger duo, Gary and Shaggy, began showing signs similar to those seen in humans with Marfan syndrome, their veterinary team started to wonder if cats could also suffer from the same condition.

    Recent findings suggest that genetic sequencing revealed that Gary and Shaggy both carried two altered copies of FBN1. In other words, they had inherited the mutation from both parents.

    Sources indicate that in humans, Marfan syndrome typically develops when a person inherits one disease-causing copy of the gene. Having two altered copies is exceptionally rare and can be associated with more severe disease.

    So the brothers presented researchers with an interesting puzzle.

    Their particular genetic variant didn't completely prevent the gene from functioning. Instead, it partially disrupted how the gene's instructions were processed, allowing some normal fibrillin-1 function to remain, which may explain why Gary and Shaggy survived into adulthood despite carrying two copies of the variant.

    Their genetic instructions weren't simply switched on or off; it was something in between, which may help explain why the brothers developed the way they did.

    It has been revealed that genes rarely behave like a tidy set of instructions. The effects of a genetic change depend on the specific variant involved and how it affects the resulting protein. Sometimes, a seemingly insignificant variation can have catastrophic consequences, altering the way the body functions.

    The case of Gary and Shaggy is undeniably rare, and Marfan syndrome is unlikely to find its way onto the list of common feline diseases. However, in diagnosing and documenting the condition, veterinarians have something they didn't have before: a confirmed case of feline Marfan syndrome to help recognize, investigate, and compare with future cases.

    These findings may help veterinary teams identify similar cases and better understand how particular FBN1 variants affect cats. They also demonstrate the value of bringing clinicians, genetic researchers, and pet parents together when a case doesn't fit neatly into an existing diagnosis.

    Gary and Shaggy's shared genetic variant offered researchers a valuable opportunity to investigate the relationship between their physical features and the underlying condition.

    Their owner, Nicole Desmond, also contributed to this process, and Cornell has highlighted the case as an example of how pet parents can collaborate with veterinary and genetic experts to advance knowledge that may eventually benefit other animals.

    Sources indicate that even more importantly, Nicole loved the unique feline brothers with her whole heart. Vets did not expect either cat to survive for long, but they defied the odds. Gary was 6 years old when he passed away in July 2024, and in November 2025, at the incredible age of 7, Shaggy joined his brother across the rainbow bridge.

    It has been revealed that and that's one of the interesting things about veterinary medicine. Not every discovery starts with a large clinical trial or a disease affecting thousands of patients. Sometimes, it begins with two unusual kittens and a veterinary team willing to keep asking questions.

    It has been revealed that the rarity of this case means we donât necessarily have to think the worst when we see a long-legged kitten; itâs far more likely that theyâre simply long-limbed and not harboring a rare genetic disorder. However, it reminds us to pay attention to the bigger picture, bring unusual findings to the veterinarian's attention, and not automatically assume that two seemingly unrelated problems have nothing to do with each other.

    Sometimes, a strange-looking kitten is simply a strange-looking kitten.

    And sometimes, those extra-long legs are the first clue to a genetic story that researchers have never documented in cats before.

    According to recent reports, dogs are easy to love but, on occasion, are also surprisingly difficult to live with. Barking for no reason. The leash pulling that turns a simple walk into a tug-of-war. Turning the most expensive thing in the room into a chew toyâ¦.

    Sources indicate that most dog owners have dealt with at least one of these behaviors, and itâs tempting to see them simply as bad habits. But the truth is, there is often a reason behind these irritating habits. Dogs communicate through behavior, and what looks like a nuisance is sometimes a symptom of an unmet need. The trouble is that we often get distracted by tackling that symptom when we really need to dig deeper.

    Understanding what is driving an annoying or unwanted behavior can make it much easier to address.

    Sources indicate that dogs bark for many reasons, including boredom, anxiety, fear, a perceived threat, or a desire for attention. Any dog can develop a barking habit, regardless of size.

    Industry observers note that the key is identifying what triggers it. Boredom-related barking may improve with more exercise and mental stimulation, while anxiety or fear-based barking generally requires a more structured approach. Teaching a reliable "quiet" command and avoiding accidentally rewarding attention-seeking barking can also help.

    Naturally vigilant dogs that spend their days standing guard at windows and alerting you to every passerby or suspicious-looking trash can may become less anxious if you block or obscure their view of the street. Limiting access to front-facing rooms or applying privacy film to windows can be a simple solution â if they canât see it, they stop worrying about it.

    Chewing is normal for dogs, particularly teething puppies, but it becomes a problem when furniture, clothing, carpets, or walls become the preferred targets.

    Boredom and anxiety can contribute to destructive chewing, as can a lack of appropriate outlets. Keeping suitable chew toys available, putting valuable items out of reach, and managing the environment while the dog learns what is acceptable can help redirect the habit.

    According to recent reports, A dog that greets visitors by launching itself at them has usually learned that jumping gets a response. Even pushing the dog away or telling it to stop can give them the attention theyâre seeking.

    Ignoring the jumping and rewarding calm, four-paws-on-the-floor behavior teaches the dog that staying down gets the better response. Giving the dog an alternative behavior, such as sitting, can make the lesson clearer.

    When faced with a friendly jumping dog, try the following:.

    Keep your arms crossed, mouth closed, and eyes averted.

    Turn your back, and walk away if they keep jumping.

    Ignore them until they are calm and ready to listen to your command.

    Industry observers note that dogs beg because it has worked before. Even one successful attempt at getting food from the table can establish the habit, making it particularly difficult to break.

    Feeding the dog before your mealtimes can reduce the motivation to beg, while teaching it to settle in a designated spot gives it something else to do. The biggest challenge is consistency. Giving in occasionally can keep the behavior going.

    Table scraps can also pose health risks because some common human foods are harmful to dogs, while regular extras can contribute to obesity.

    According to recent reports, leash pulling can make an otherwise enjoyable walk exhausting. Dogs often pull because they are excited and have not learned that pulling does not make the walk happen faster.

    Loose-leash training takes patience. Stopping whenever the leash becomes tight and continuing only when it becomes slack teaches the dog what behavior allows the walk to continue. Rewarding the dog for walking beside the handler can reinforce the lesson, while a well-fitted harness may provide additional control during training.

    Different dogs need different equipment, and what works for a small dog is not necessarily going to be suitable for a large one. Talk to your vet about the safest and most effective option for you and your dog.

    Poor recall is frustrating, but it can also be dangerous if your dog runs towards traffic or another dog.

    Training should start in areas with few distractions before gradually becoming more challenging. High-value rewards can make coming back more appealing, while using the recall command for unpleasant situations can create a negative association that undermines the training.

    Digging is instinctive for many dogs and can also be linked to boredom or excess energy. Trying to eliminate the behavior completely may not be the most practical approach; redirection has a much higher chance of success.

    Industry observers note that create a designated digging area, such as a sandbox or corner of the yard, making sure there is a clear distinction between this and the rest of the garden. It may be unsightly, but laying down some temporary netting or a similar obstacle in the rest of the yard can help teach your dog where they can and cannot dig. Burying toys or treats there can make the spot more appealing, while increasing daily activity may reduce the urge to dig elsewhere.

    It has been revealed that some dogs struggle when left alone. The resulting distress can include destructive behavior, excessive barking, and other difficult behaviors.

    Gradually getting a dog used to being alone, starting with very short absences and slowly increasing them, is an evidence-based approach. Providing a comfortable, safe space can also help.

    Avoid making a fuss of your dog when leaving the house or on your return â your comings and goings should become part of an ordinary day, not an event. More severe cases of separation anxiety may require veterinary input or help from a behaviorist.

    Sources indicate that aggression can have many possible causes, including fear, poor socialization, pain, territorial behavior, or negative past experiences. Because the appropriate response depends on the cause, this is one behavior where professional help is particularly crucial.

    A veterinary examination can help rule out an underlying medical problem, including pain. A qualified trainer or behaviorist can then help address the behavior using approaches such as positive reinforcement, desensitization, and counterconditioning. Punishment can make aggression worse rather than better.

    Occasional accidents can happen, but frequent or sudden indoor elimination deserves attention.

    For dogs that are still learning, regular bathroom breaks and immediate positive reinforcement for going outside provide the foundation for housetraining. Enzymatic cleaners are useful for removing waste odors that can otherwise encourage a dog to return to the same spot.

    If a previously house-trained dog suddenly begins having accidents, a check-up at the vet is appropriate to check for a possible medical cause.

    It has been revealed that barking, chewing, jumping, digging, and the other behaviors on this list may be frustrating, but they rarely happen without a reason. Looking at what a dog is trying to communicate can reveal whether it needs more activity, clearer training, or a different kind of attention.

    Addressing the underlying matter rather than simply trying to stop the behavior can make the problem easier to manage and help strengthen the relationship between you and your dog.

    We all know that feline behavior can be somewhat unpredictable. Just when you think youâve got it all figured out, a cat is already three steps ahead of you. But thereâs a massive difference between normal feline quirks and uncharacteristic aggression.

    Industry observers note that A cat that has always been gentle and suddenly starts lashing out may be reacting to something in its environment, changing hormones, pain, or a health problem. Aggression has many causes, from fear and frustration to competition with other cats. Understanding what has changed can help identify the cause and determine the best way to respond.

    Unneutered male cats may fight over access to females, particularly when several cats are competing for mates in the same area. When a female cat is in heat, she may attract multiple males, making fights more likely.

    Female cats can also behave differently during heat cycles. Many become unusually affectionate and demanding of attention, while others may become irritable or aggressive. Hormonal changes can also affect how they interact with other cats, particularly other females.

    Sources indicate that spaying/neutering is an vital aspect of taking care of a cat. Not only does it help to minimize aggression and friction between cats, but it also prevents unwanted litters and helps reduce the risk of certain diseases.

    Industry observers note that pain can make even a normally friendly cat lash out. A cat may react aggressively if someone touches a sore area or approaches when it is feeling unwell.

    Urinary tract disease can make a cat pretty miserable, and males in particular are vulnerable to urinary blockages, which are extremely painful and can become life-threatening. A cat that is straining to urinate or unable to pass urine needs emergency veterinary attention.

    Infections, injuries, arthritis, and cancer are often painful but difficult to recognize from the outside. If aggression appears suddenly or seems linked to discomfort, a veterinary examination is an important first step.

    It has been revealed that A frightened cat may respond aggressively when startled, even if it is usually relaxed and friendly. A sudden noise, an unfamiliar person, or another threatening experience can trigger a defensive reaction.

    Ongoing stress can also contribute to aggression. Cats that feel unsafe in their surroundings may remain on edge and react defensively to people or animals around them.

    It has been revealed that every cat should have access to a quiet, comfortable place where it can retreat without being disturbed. Giving a frightened cat space can help it feel more secure.

    It has been revealed that not every aggressive-looking interaction is driven by anger or fear. Play helps cats practise their hunting skills, and some become too rough when playing with people or other animals.

    In a recent development, however, rough play should not be encouraged because biting and scratching can cause injuries. Rewarding gentle play and redirecting a cat toward appropriate toys can help it learn more acceptable ways to use its energy.

    Cats can be protective of their territory, so the arrival of another animal may trigger aggression. The newcomer could be a fresh cat or dog in the household, or an outdoor cat that has started visiting the yard.

    Sometimes, owners may not even realize another cat is nearby. Seeing or smelling an unfamiliar animal can leave a cat agitated, causing it to react to other pets or people.

    Aggressive behavior plus inappropriate urination and scent-marking are not uncommon when a cat feels its territory is under threat.

    A cat that becomes frustrated by something it cannot reach may take that frustration out on another target. This is known as redirected aggression.

    For example, a cat might become agitated after seeing another cat outside, then lash out at a person or pet nearby. The target may have done nothing wrong and simply been in the wrong place at the wrong time.

    Giving an agitated cat time and space to calm down is safer than trying to handle it immediately.

    According to recent reports, cats living together usually have established social relationships, and introducing a upcoming pet tends to upset the status quo. A certain amount of fighting and posturing is to be expected as the cats adjust to the change, but escalating aggression or bullying of one cat should be addressed.

    Introducing a new animal gradually can help reduce conflict. Cats should have time to become familiar with each other without being forced into close contact before they are ready.

    Some cats seem to enjoy attention but suddenly bite or scratch once petting begins. A cat may become overstimulated by touch, or it may simply want to be near a person without being handled.

    According to recent reports, watch for signs of discomfort, such as flattened ears or a flicking tail. If a cat seems agitated, stop petting and give it space. Treats can reward calm interactions when the cat is comfortable.

    Aggression can be difficult for a household to manage, but many causes can be addressed with patience and the right approach. Rewarding calm behavior, avoiding known triggers, and providing a safe place to retreat can all help.

    Industry observers note that the first step is to work out why the cat is behaving differently. If the aggression is sudden, it may be linked to pain or illness, so you should always consult a veterinarian before treating it as a behavioral matter. Once medical causes are excluded, look for changes â both indoors and outside the home â that might be affecting your cat.

    Simple steps like providing extra hiding places, calming aids, and adapting handling techniques can go a long way to reducing feline aggression.

    My cat, Mitzi, is 16 years and 8 months old. She has early-stage kidney disease and hyperthyroidism, which she is on medication for. About 2 months ago, she became deaf, and since then has refused to leave the master bedroom. I have moved her water bowl and litter box there and feed her there.

    Is there anything I can do to get her to come out?â.

    At her age, sweet Mitzi has certainly earned the right to enjoy her golden years at her own pace, but I can imagine it is difficult to see her withdraw from the rest of the house, especially when you remember how she used to move around. However, I would not necessarily interpret her reluctance to leave the bedroom as something we need to correct. Losing her hearing can be quite disorienting. Imagine walking into a room where you can no longer hear footsteps, familiar voices, or the little sounds that help you understand what is happening around you. For Mitzi, the bedroom may now feel like her safest little world, where everything is familiar and predictable.

    Sources indicate that I actually think you have done a wonderful job adapting her environment by bringing her food, water, and litter box closer. Rather than encouraging her to leave right away, I would focus on helping her feel confident enough to explore if she wishes. You could start by sitting with her near the bedroom doorway, offering a favorite treat or a little affection. Gradually place treats a short distance beyond the door, allowing her to decide whether she wants to investigate.

    Take care to only approach her within her visual field, avoid startling her while she sleeps, and keep pathways clear and nonslip. Think of it as extending her latest world one comfortable step at a time, rather than asking her to return to her old routine.

    According to recent reports, there is one thing I would not overlook, though. Mitzi has both chronic kidney disease and hyperthyroidism, and at her age, reduced mobility or withdrawal can also be associated with arthritis, high blood pressure, visual changes, or inadequate control of her thyroid disease. I would recommend a senior cat veterinary checkup that includes blood pressure measurement, assessment for arthritis, and follow-up kidney and thyroid testing. Sometimes what looks like a behavioral change is actually a senior cat quietly telling us that they are in pain and something does not feel quite right.

    It has been revealed that most importantly, please do not feel that you are encouraging a bad habit by keeping her essentials in the bedroom. You are adapting her home to meet her changing needs, and that is a beautiful expression of your love and care for her. If the bedroom is where Mitzi feels safe, eats well, drinks, uses her litter box, and enjoys your manufacturer, that can be a perfectly good quality of life.

    At this stage, happiness is not measured by how much of the house she explores, but by how comfortable and secure she feels in the little world she chooses.
