    When my boss passed away, I took in his older Red Heeler, Bob, so he didnât end up in the pound. I've been giving him turkey tail for his lumps, and he is overweight.

    Itâs hard to walk him when it's 100 degrees out. For the last couple of months, he has been drinking so much water and urinating way more than usual. He mostly stays inside, and when I take him out to pee, the first thing when he comes back in is head for the water bowl, like he wants to replace what he just got rid of!

    Any suggestions on what I could try?â.

    Sources indicate that you have done something very kind by giving Bob a home after losing his person. It sounds like he is a senior boy who has already been through a lot, and it is wonderful that he has someone looking out for him. The increased drinking and urination you are seeing, especially since this has been going on for a couple of months, is something I would have checked rather than assuming it is just his age or the hot weather. Older dogs can develop several conditions that cause this combination of signs, including diabetes, kidney disease, and Cushing's disease.

    Recent findings suggest that I would schedule a veterinary examination and ask for some basic lab work, particularly blood tests and urinalysis. These can give us information that we simply cannot get from looking at Bob. Bloodwork can tell us about his blood glucose, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, and other changes that may help identify what is going on. A urine sample is just as valuable. It can show whether his kidneys are concentrating the urine properly, and can also detect glucose, ketones, protein, blood, inflammation, and other abnormalities. Depending on those results, his veterinarian may recommend some additional tests.

    Please do not limit his water, even if it seems like he is drinking right back what he just urinated. In many of these conditions, the excessive thirst is the body's way of trying to replace fluid that is being lost. Taking water away can actually make him dehydrated and much sicker. Keep fresh water available at all times, and because of the heat, try to take him out during the cooler parts of the day. If you can, measuring approximately how much water he drinks in 24 hours would also be very helpful information for his veterinarian.

    I would also recommend that he has the lumps properly checked rather than relying on turkey tail or other supplements. Some lumps are harmless, but others can be more serious, and we cannot tell the difference just by feeling or looking at them. A fine needle aspiration can often collect cells from a lump with very little discomfort and may give the veterinarian a much better idea of what it is. With Bob being overweight and having difficulty walking in the heat, getting his medical issues sorted out first will also make it much safer to work on his weight and mobility.

    He has clearly found someone who cares about him, and sometimes the most loving thing we can do for an older dog is simply to find out what his body is trying to tell us.

    According to recent reports, every time the topic of vaccines comes up, thereâs always someone who questions whether our pets really need them. Asking questions about medical care is perfectly reasonable (in fact, informed pet parents should!), but dismissing vaccination without understanding the risks is another story.

    In a recent development, rabies is a perfect example. This is not some historical disease or something that only affects animals in remote areas or underdeveloped countries. It can infect mammals, including our own cats, dogs, and even us. Whatâs even scarier is that once the clinical signs appear, rabies is almost always fatal, making prevention essential.

    Industry observers note that recent events in Quebec offer a timely reminder. Amid an emerging wildlife outbreak, three domestic cats tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies in 2026. Although these numbers pale in comparison to the number of infected wildlife recorded since December 20241, it demonstrates how a disease circulating in wild animals can reach our pets.

    Industry observers note that and this isn't just a Canadian concern. Rabies variants and wildlife risks differ by region, but keeping pets appropriately vaccinated is a responsibility shared by pet parents everywhere.

    Despite its name, raccoon-strain rabies isn't exclusive to raccoons; they are simply the reservoir species of this particular variant of the rabies virus. Skunks and other mammals â including cats â can also become infected.

    Recent findings suggest that rabies attacks the central nervous system. It spreads mainly through the bite of an infected animal, when virus-containing saliva enters the body. Saliva can also transmit the virus if it reaches an open wound, the eyes, nose, or mouth.

    Raccoon rabies had been eliminated in Quebec following an outbreak between 2006 and 2009, but the virus resurfaced in 2024. Since then, more outbreaks have appeared, and case numbers have climbed sharply in 2026, particularly in MontÃ©rÃ©gie. By October 29, 328 animals had tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies across the province. The three infected cats are examples of how a virus circulating in wildlife can also reach our pets, even though cats are not the main reservoir responsible for spreading this variant.

    It has been revealed that cats are naturally curious, territorial predators. They investigate unfamiliar scents, watch moving animals, explore hidden spaces, and sometimes pursue creatures that would be better left alone. These behaviors are normal expressions of feline biology, not evidence that a cat is being reckless.

    Industry observers note that unfortunately, wildlife encounters can turn dangerous very quickly. A raccoon searching for food near a house may cross paths with an outdoor cat. A skunk hiding beneath a shed may be investigated by a curious feline. Even a sick or disoriented wild animal can catch a cat's attention, and one of the hallmarks of rabies infection in wild animals is a reduced fear of humans and predators as the infection attacks the nervous system. And cats being cats, curiosity can get them into trouble! These encounters don't just happen deep in the woods. A backyard, garage, or garden fence can be enough.

    One of the infected cats was believed to have contracted rabies after contact with a wild animal. Another case led to three people receiving preventive treatment following possible exposure.

    Rabies doesn't always turn an animal into a movie villain, either. Early signs can be subtle, which is why recognizing unusual behavior and reporting possible exposure is so important.

    It has been revealed that when people think of rabies, they often picture a snarling animal, dripping saliva, and attacking everything in sight. Hollywood certainly loves that version! Unfortunately, rabies doesn't always come with such obvious special effects.

    In cats, the first signs can be surprisingly subtle. A normally friendly kitty may suddenly become grumpy, hide more than usual, vocalize differently, lose interest in food, or behave in ways that seem completely out of character. Since cats are already experts at keeping their humans guessing, a sudden behavior change can sometimes be easy to dismiss. But when a cat starts acting noticeably different from their usual, wonderfully weird self, it's worth paying attention.

    Recent findings suggest that as the disease progresses, neurological signs become more apparent. Affected cats may become disoriented, walk unsteadily, have difficulty swallowing, drool excessively, develop weakness, or eventually become paralyzed. Some become unusually aggressive or sensitive to touch, sounds, and light.

    There is also a less dramatic presentation called paralytic rabies, sometimes referred to as âdumb rabiesâ. Instead of becoming aggressive, affected animals may become unusually quiet, weak, or withdrawn. Difficulty swallowing, a drooping jaw, and progressive paralysis can follow. So no, a rabid animal doesn't necessarily look like it's auditioning for a horror movie.

    Of course, these signs can also occur with other neurological conditions, injuries, and intoxications. Nobody should attempt to diagnose rabies based on behavior alone. A cat showing sudden, unexplained neurological changes needs prompt veterinary attention, particularly if wildlife exposure is possible.

    It has been revealed that here's another catch: rabies can take weeks, sometimes even months, to show itself. A cat may seem perfectly fine after an encounter with an infected animal, but that doesn't mean the virus isn't already in its body. So if a possible exposure happens, don't wait for your cat to look sick before calling the vet. By then, it may be too late.

    Sadly, once rabies reaches the clinical stage, there is no cure, and the outcome is almost always fatal. That's why a suspected exposure should never be a wait-and-see situation. Don't wait for signs to appear; contact your veterinarian right away. With rabies, prevention isn't just better than treatment; it's our best chance to protect our cats in the first place.

    Sources indicate that think your indoor cat doesn't need a rabies vaccine? Think again! Indoor cats have fewer opportunities to encounter wildlife, but escapes happen, doors get left open, and sometimes wildlife finds its way indoors. Nobody aims these little adventures, least of all the cat!

    In a recent development, rabies vaccination is also required by law for cats in many countries and jurisdictions. Even where it isn't mandatory, keeping your cat vaccinated is an vital part of preventive care. Ask your veterinarian about the appropriate schedule for your cat.

    According to recent reports, and remember, vaccination doesn't mean ignoring a possible exposure. If your vaccinated cat is bitten by a potentially rabid animal, contact your veterinarian right away.

    In a recent development, if your cat is bitten or scratched by a wild animal, contact your veterinarian immediately, even if your cat seems perfectly fine. Bite wounds can hide beneath all that lovely fur, and waiting for signs to appear is not an option.

    According to recent reports, keep your cat away from other animals and don't try to catch or handle the wild animal. Report suspicious wildlife to local authorities and let trained professionals deal with it.

    Recent findings suggest that if a person is bitten or scratched, or infected saliva enters an open wound or contacts the eyes, nose, or mouth, wash the area thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes and seek medical attention immediately. Post-exposure treatment can prevent rabies from developing, so don't delay.

    And please, leave dead wildlife alone. No bare-handed investigations or impromptu rescue missions!

    Sources indicate that quebec is also fighting the outbreak through wildlife surveillance and vaccination campaigns using vaccine baits. These efforts help protect wild animals and reduce further spread.

    In a recent development, cats will be cats. A rustling bush can become the most fascinating thing in the universe, and a passing raccoon may look like an invitation to investigate. We can't blame them for being curious. We can give them safer ways to enjoy their adventures.

    HELP WANTED: Scientists Seeking Senior Dogs To Unlock the Secrets of Aging

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

    What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

    Industry observers note that that is the opportunity behind a major clinical trial from the Dog Aging Project, a research collaboration focused on giving us a better understanding of canine aging. The project is at the moment looking for older, healthy dogs to participate in the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs, better known as TRIAD.

    This study is attracting renewed attention following a recent 60 Minutes report on the Dog Aging Project and its work investigating why dogs age the way they do and how their golden years might be made healthier.

    TRIAD is not simply asking how long dogs can live. Researchers are trying to understand if a medication called rapamycin can influence the aging process and improve health in older dogs.

    Recent findings suggest that rapamycin, also known as sirolimus or Rapamune, is a macrolide drug with immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. This medication has been used in human medicine for more than two decades, including in patients who have undergone kidney transplantation.

    Recent findings suggest that the interest in rapamycin and aging comes from a different area of research. Studies in laboratory organisms found that rapamycin can extend lifespan in several species, including mice, yeast, worms, and flies. Now, researchers want to find out whether those benefits could extend to our pets.

    Industry observers note that the Dog Aging Projectâs TRIAD trial is a multicenter study involving researchers and veterinary hospitals at universities across the United States, including Tufts University. The TRIAD trial is investigating whether rapamycin can influence lifespan and, importantly, promote healthy aging in companion dogs.

    For veterinary science, one of the most interesting parts of aging research is the difference between lifespan and healthspan.

    Sources indicate that lifespan is how long an animal lives. Healthspan is the portion of that life spent in good health.

    Living longer is great, but what matters just as much is how dogs feel during those extra years. More time with the family means less if a dog is struggling with chronic illness, having trouble getting around, or experiencing cognitive decline. The goal isn't just to add years to a dog's life. It's to help them enjoy more of those years feeling good.

    TRIAD is examining several areas of canine health, including cognitive function, heart function, immunity, and cancer incidence.

    The current TRIAD recruitment drive is specifically aimed at older dogs that meet the study's eligibility requirements. To be considered for the study, dogs must:.

    Be able to cooperate with examinations, including blood collection and cardiac ultrasound, without sedation.

    Have normal diagnostic findings at enrollment.

    Clinical trial sites are located throughout the United States.

    Sources indicate that for families who decide to participate, it is crucial to consider that this is a three-year commitment. During the first year, dogs receive either rapamycin or a placebo. Once that year is over, the medication stops, but the study continues. Researchers will follow the dogs for another two years to see how they age and whether any differences emerge over time. In total, owners will bring their dogs to a clinical trial site seven times during the three-year study.

    When it comes to getting older, dogs and humans have quite a lot in common. Dogs are susceptible to many of the same age-related conditions we are, including cognitive decline, arthritis, heart disease, cancer, and other chronic health problems. And since they share our homes and daily environments, a great deal of what researchers learn from studying aging in dogs can be extrapolated to humans.

    The recent 60 Minutes report touched on this connection, including research into canine dementia. It's an area worth paying attention to, especially as more dogs live into their senior years.

    Recent findings suggest that there's also a practical advantage. Dogs age much faster than humans. This allows researchers to track changes in their health over a few years instead of waiting decades. That's a big deal when you're trying to understand what happens as the body ages.

    But this isn't just about what dogs can teach us about ourselves. What researchers discover will help dogs, too.

    Aging isn't a single disease that can be treated with one medication. As dogs get older, several things can start changing at once, sometimes as a domino or cascade effect after an initial problem or illness. Maybe getting up becomes harder, walks get shorter, or a dog who's always been sharp seems a little confused. Sometimes these changes happen gradually, and it's easy to chalk them up to old age.

    The more we learn about what's actually happening in an aging dog's body, the better chance veterinarians have of spotting problems earlier and finding ways to help dogs feel good for as long as possible.

    Due to the eligibility requirements, not every dog will qualify for TRIAD, but that doesnât mean they canât contribute to canine aging research.

    The Dog Aging Project also has a broader research community known as the DAP Pack, which welcomes dogs of different ages, sizes, breeds, and backgrounds. The project explains that dogs who do not qualify for TRIAD can still make a meaningful contribution to understanding canine aging.

    Itâs important to include all kinds of dogs in this research, not just a particular breed or size. A dog's genes, lifestyle, environment, size, and even their health history can all play a role in how they age. The more variety researchers can study, the better picture they can get of why some dogs stay healthy well into their senior years while others develop health problems earlier.

    Sources indicate that when it comes to canine aging, the goal isn't just to help dogs live longer. It's to help them feel good for more of those years, stay active, and keep enjoying life with their families.

    And anyone who's lived with a senior dog knows that two dogs of the same age can be worlds apart. One 10-year-old may still be eager for walks, playtime, and whatever the family has planned that day. Another might be struggling with mobility or dealing with several health problems. So, what makes the difference?

    That's part of what makes the TRIAD study interesting. Rapamycin has shown promising results in other species, but researchers still need to find out whether it can make a meaningful difference in dogs. That's a question that needs to be tested, and your pup may be part of this!

    For owners of senior dogs, taking part in research like this is a chance to help scientists get some answers. What they learn could help us better understand why dogs age differently and what might help them stay healthier as they get older.

    So, if you have a pup in their golden years, check out the Dog Aging Project and see how your four-legged friend might become part of this research.

    • Nobody enjoys thinking about serious illness in a pet, and itâs natural to want to look the other way.
    • Heart problems are notoriously hard to spot in cats, even during a routine health check, because the usual signs, like a murmur, donât always show up during an exam.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

    Nobody enjoys thinking about serious illness in a pet, and itâs natural to want to look the other way. But considering many serious feline health conditions respond well to early intervention, a little knowledge can go a long way. Here are eight of the most serious, what they tend to look like, and practical steps that can help lower the risk. The aim isnât to worry anyone, just to help owners feel prepared.

    Heart problems are notoriously hard to spot in cats, even during a routine health check, because the usual signs, like a murmur, donât always show up during an exam. The most common form of cardiac disease â hypertrophic cardiomyopathy â causes the heart muscle to thicken so it canât work as well, and it can cause sudden death. Vets rely on heart scans, chest X-rays, and blood tests to discover heart disease.

    Lowering the risk: Genetics play a big part, so anyone buying a kitten from a breeder should ask whether the parentsâ hearts have been checked, particularly if your breed of choice is one with a higher incidence of cardiac disease, like purebred Maine Coons, Siamese, Sphynx, Ragdoll, and Burmese. A high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet formulated for cats is a vital ingredient in promoting heart health. Cat food must contain the amino acid taurine because cats cannot make it themselves, and a diet lacking this essential nutrient is a fast track to heart disease.

    According to recent reports, kidney disease is common in older cats. The kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter waste, which reveals up as drinking and urinating more, tiredness, weight loss, and a scruffy coat. It can also lead to high blood pressure and low red blood cell counts, which cause pale gums, weakness, and fast breathing.

    Lowering the risk: Although kidney disease canât be entirely prevented, regular checkups with blood and urine tests can catch changes early. A balanced diet helps, and maximizing a catâs water intake by feeding wet food and providing a range of enticing water options can make a significant difference.

    Recent findings suggest that feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) is prevalent in cat populations around the world and is the most common cause of feline cancer. FeLV attacks the bone marrow, and the clinical signs of infection can be quite variable, but often include lethargy, weight loss, poor appetite, and weakness. Because FeLV cripples the immune system, affected cats are more susceptible to disease, and an otherwise simple infection can be deadly.

    Sources indicate that lowering the risk: Vaccination is the best protection. Keeping cats indoors and away from possibly infected cats helps, as does quarantining newcomers and regularly cleaning dishes, toys, bedding, and litter boxes.

    This is the most common hormone disease in cats, affecting about 10% of cats over age ten. It can lead to heart problems, kidney disease, blindness, and death. Cats lose weight promptly despite a huge appetite, and some suddenly go blind because of high blood pressure. Fortunately, the outlook is good with treatment, including medication, surgery, or radioactive iodine.

    Lowering the risk: Hyperthyroidism canât be prevented, so spotting changes early and getting annual blood screening are the best weapons.

    Up to one in a hundred cats develops diabetes in their lifetime, either because they donât make enough insulin or canât use it properly. Left untreated, it can cause serious complications. Signs include weight loss, drinking and urinating more, accidents outside the litter box, and bloody urine. Treatment is usually insulin injections, but if caught early, it can sometimes be managed through diet.

    Lowering the risk: Feeding a high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet with low carbohydrate levels can help reduce the risks. The most common form of diabetes in cats is Type 2 (insulin resistance) and the best way to avoid this disease is by maintaining a lean, healthy body condition.

    Industry observers note that rabies is almost always fatal, and cats are the domestic animal most likely to get it. It spreads through bites and scratches, often from wildlife such as bats, skunks, raccoons, and foxes. Some infected cats become withdrawn, others irritable or aggressive, and drooling and wide pupils are common. It is dangerous for people too.

    Lowering the risk: Vaccines protect for one to three years. If contact with rabies is suspected, veterinary attention must be sought immediately. The disease is invariably fatal once clinical signs of rabies appear, so donât wait.

    Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP) is caused by a mutated form of feline coronavirus. Early signs are mild, such as tiredness, but many cats develop a swollen belly from fluid, and it can progress fast. Until recently, FIP was almost always fatal, though newer treatments are changing this.

    Sources indicate that lowering the risk: Good hygiene between cats and isolating newcomers until theyâre healthy reduce exposure. Keeping cats healthy and up to date on other vaccines may also help.

    Spread by mosquitoes, heartworms are less common in cats than in dogs, but they can still cause serious disease, including sudden death. Wheezing and coughing are the most common signs, and the infection is hard to detect.

    Lowering the risk: A monthly preventive is the best defense. If you live in an area where heartworm is present, it takes only one mosquito, so even indoor cats can be exposed.

    Not every disease on this list can be prevented, but many can be avoided or managed simply by providing your cat with a high-quality diet and keeping up with regular vet checks. Blood and urine tests, appropriate vaccines, and monthly flea, tick, and heartworm protection all help, and keeping cats indoors lowers exposure to injury and illness. Catching problems early is often what makes treatment most effective, and a vet can help tailor a strategy for each cat.

    Halloween packs a steady stream of costumed strangers and bowls of candy into a single evening, and for dogs that combination carries more hazards than most people expect. Most of the risks are easy to avoid with a little planning, and several of them start well before the first trick-or-treater arrives at the door. These precautions help keep dogs out of trouble while the rest of the household enjoys Halloween.

    Sources indicate that halloween candy can be dangerous for dogs, and the wrappers create an additional hazard. Certain ingredients in sweets, including chocolate and xylitol, can be toxic to dogs, while swallowed wrappers can cause choking or digestive problems.

    In a recent development, keeping candy in a closed container at home is a good starting point, but the risk doesn't end at the front door. Keeping a close eye on what a dog sniffs or picks up can help prevent an unwanted snack from turning into a veterinary emergency.

    Recent findings suggest that costumes for dogs can be adorable and hilarious, but only if the dog agrees. Not every dog feels happy playing dress-up, so itâs vital to pay attention to how they respond.

    A costume should fit comfortably without restricting movement or creating opportunities for the dog to become tangled. An outfit that fit last year may now be too tight, while one bought for a puppy to grow into could be awkward or unsafe in the meantime.

    Before heading out or welcoming visitors, check that the costume fits properly and your pup can walk comfortably in it.

    A Halloween costume can look adorable on a dog, but wearing one safely requires supervision. Some dogs become fascinated by their outfits and start chewing at loose fabric or accessories, potentially creating a choking hazard.

    Industry observers note that there's no reason every dog has to avoid costumes, provided the outfit is comfortable and the dog tolerates wearing it. But if the dog needs to be left alone, take the costume off. It's a simple precaution that reduces the chance of an otherwise harmless outfit causing trouble.

    Industry observers note that halloween can be overwhelming for dogs that struggle with noise, unfamiliar people, or constant activity. Trick-or-treaters arrive throughout the evening, and costumes can make even familiar surroundings feel different.

    Sources indicate that A dog that becomes overexcited or anxious may benefit from having somewhere quiet to retreat. A separate room with a comfortable bed, fresh water, and familiar toys can provide a welcome break from the commotion.

    Make sure visitors understand that the dog shouldn't be disturbed if it chooses to settle somewhere away from the activity.

    It has been revealed that jack-o'-lanterns, lights, and other Halloween decorations can make a home feel festive, but curious dogs may see them as things to investigate or chew. Keep decorations out of reach, particularly anything that could be harmful if swallowed.

    Real candles inside pumpkins also pose a risk if a dog knocks one over. Battery-operated alternatives are a safer choice, especially in areas where pets can wander freely.

    Glow sticks and glowing bracelets help make children more visible during evening trick-or-treating, but their bright colors and flexible shapes can also attract a dog's attention.

    The liquid inside can cause irritation and may be harmful if swallowed. A dog that bites through a glow stick could end up ingesting the contents, so these items should be kept well away from curious mouths.

    In a recent development, check the ground during walks, too, particularly on Halloween night when discarded glow sticks and bracelets may be lying around. If a dog chews or swallows one, contact a vet for advice.

    Handing out candy can mean opening the front door dozens of times in a single evening. For a dog that's curious, excitable, or easily frightened, those repeated opportunities can make an escape more likely.

    Closing the door between visitors helps prevent a dog from slipping outside unnoticed. Another option is to step outside to greet trick-or-treaters and close the door behind you.

    According to recent reports, keeping the dog in a separate room during busy periods adds another layer of protection. It also reduces the chance of a dog becoming startled by costumed visitors appearing at the entrance.

    An identification tag and microchip are always a good idea, but they become particularly vital on a night when doors are opening frequently, and unusual sights may startle a dog.

    Industry observers note that if a dog escapes, an ID tag with current contact details gives whoever finds it a straightforward way to get in touch. A microchip provides another means of identifying the dog and helping it return home.

    It has been revealed that check that the dog's tag is attached securely and that the contact information associated with its microchip is up to date. These small steps can make a significant difference if a dog gets loose.

    It has been revealed that halloween can be stressful and dangerous for dogs, but it doesnât have to be. Keeping candy secured, choosing comfortable costumes, providing a quiet retreat, and making sure the front door stays closed can prevent many of the problems associated with the holiday.

    It's also worth remembering that dogs may react unpredictably to unfamiliar costumes and unusual activity, even if they're normally relaxed around visitors. Staying attentive from the first doorbell to the last helps keep the evening enjoyable for everyone, including the four-legged members of the household.

    Maybe it is having a family that loves them. Maybe it is a warm bed, a full bowl, and a safe place to sleep. Or maybe luck is something a little more fundamental: having people who see you as an individual and take the time to understand what you need.

    At Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption Center near Lake Chapala, Mexico, the dogs may still be waiting for permanent homes, but in the meantime, they are surrounded by caring people who show up for them day after day.

    At Lucky Dog, everyone has a unique way to help and collaborate.

    Some volunteers walk dogs. Others train them, clean their enclosures, help with fundraising, or coordinate veterinary care. Some foster dogs in their homes. Others help with the less visible work that keeps the center running.

    When I visited Lucky Dog, I arrived with Mark and Nancy. Mark helped build the Thursday volunteer group, bringing together people who wanted to help in different ways.

    It has been revealed that âI've gotten to know a lot of people who want to help, and somehow Thursday became our day. We have our group, and everybody has something they can do. You don't have to do everything. You just have to show up and help with what you can.â.

    Industry observers note that mark has an injured knee, and at the moment, he cannot walk the long distances over cobblestone roads around the center, but he and Nancy have their own important role. They bring chairs into the enclosures and spend about 20 minutes with the dogs, offering pats, treats, kind words, and ear scratches. The dogs happily settle in beside them.

    It has been revealed that different volunteer groups cover each day of the week. Some take dogs for walks, while others help with training, cleaning, maintenance, administration, or fundraising.

    It has been revealed that that Thursday, each person simply did what they came to do. For the dogs, every part of that effort is what makes them feel lucky.

    During the day, the dogs stay in pairs in larger enclosures. They are taken out for long walks or playtime in the larger garden areas around the center. In the mornings and evenings, Valentin, one of only two paid workers at the rescue, moves the dogs between their daytime and nighttime enclosures and feeds them breakfast and dinner. During the day, volunteers help with walks, playtime, training, and puppy lunchtime.

    At night, the dogs return to smaller individual enclosures.

    When a dog needs medical attention, a veterinarian comes to the center to examine and treat them. Volunteers then follow the veterinarian's instructions and continue treatment.

    From Valentin's morning and evening routine to the volunteers who walk, train, feed, and care for the dogs, many people contribute to a Lucky Dog's day.

    The roots of today's Lucky Dog Rescue go back to 2001, when Geoffrey Kaye and Lourdes Avila started an animal shelter in Riberas del Pilar. When the shelter closed in 2012, the commitment to helping the area's dogs continued. Volunteers regrouped with veterinarian Dr. Antonio Ladron, and in December 2012, Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption opened its doors.

    Since then, the center has continued caring for abandoned and abused dogs while helping prepare them for permanent homes.

    In 2025, Lucky Dog took in 23 dogs and placed 23 through adoption or transfer. Approximately 35 new volunteers joined, with around 30 committing to weekly shifts. The center's intended capacity is 22 dogs, yet its average monthly census was close to 30 during the year.

    Those numbers give you some idea of the work happening behind every individual dog.

    Recent findings suggest that spicy is dog-reactive and needs to be housed separately from other dogs. Mark has developed a close relationship with her, and she has a very clear opinion about where his attention should go.

    Industry observers note that âSpicy loves me, and she is not happy when she sees me go into a different enclosure to pet another dog,â Mark stated. âI have to do it in a way that I hide from her so she canât see or she won't stop barking.â.

    It is a sweet story, but it also demonstrates why understanding each dog's personality matters.

    According to recent reports, hope Procops, who works as a groundskeeper and guard at Lucky Dog, understands how important volunteers are to organizations like this. Itâs not just about the day-to-day tasks. Itâs about looking after the dogs in their care and preparing them for life beyond the shelter. She says the goal of Lucky Dog Rescue is âto ensure all the dogs in our care are kept healthy, loved, socialized, and given the best chance to find their forever homes.â.

    Camille Short is in charge of training volunteers and dogs at Lucky Dog. Her approach goes beyond teaching basic commands. The goal is to help dogs develop skills that can help them succeed in a home.

    Recent findings suggest that three young siblings, Sasha, Stephanie, and Sergio, were already showing how quickly puppies can learn. They knew how to sit and lie down on command, and were learning to walk with their harnesses. They were highly motivated by treats and, judging by the puppy kisses, equally enthusiastic about people.

    It has been revealed that two of the puppies, Stephanie and Sergio, have already been chosen by families; their adoption papers are signed and ready. Sasha remains available for adoption.

    Recent findings suggest that as for Spicy, she arrived at Lucky Dog in 2022 and has been waiting for her latest home ever since. Initially anxious and mistrustful, she has come a long way with the daily attention and interactions she receives from volunteers. Now, Spicy is looking for a confident new best friend.

    âEverything nice with a little bit of spice,â says Camille of Spicy. âShe loves people and attention but is selective about her four-legged friends.â.

    Some dogs find their people promptly. Others need more time, medical care, or someone who understands their particular personality. Until then, their days continue with walks, play, veterinary care, clean enclosures, treats, kind words, and volunteers who take the time to understand them.

    Vice President of Lucky Dog Rescue, Darryl Painter, describes the mission as:.

    âImproving animal welfare in Lake Chapala via rescue, adoption, community, and fostering.â.

    Industry observers note that the sense of community was tangible during my visit, but perhaps what stayed with me most was how much we humans and dogs have in common. We are all sentient beings, and in our own ways, we all need to be acknowledged, accepted for who we are, and given the opportunity to love and be loved.

    Sources indicate that at Lucky Dog, those needs are met in many different ways. A walk, a clean enclosure, a treat, a kind word, or simply having someone take the time to know an individual dog.

    Maybe that is what makes them lucky.

    Not just having people who care for them, but having people who take the time to know them.

    And that is something anyone can do. Whether it is volunteering, fostering, sponsoring, or simply offering time and attention, there is a way to help.

    And every morning, people arrive.

    And perhapsâ¦that is what makes these dogs lucky.

    We often turn to art for pleasure, curiosity, or a feeling we canât quite put into words. A painting catches our attention; a sculpture makes us pause. But art inspiring us to adopt a dog? Now thereâs a plot twist.

    The Rescue Collection is an exciting project created through a collaboration between The Sato Project, creative agencies BLKJ Havas Singapore and Havas New York, and Brooklynâs Powerhouse Arts. The program brings adoptable dogs into the art gallery and uses observations of their responses to create individual artistic profiles.     Itâs an unusual approach to a familiar challenge: helping rescue dogs get noticed in a crowded adoption landscape.

    It has been revealed that at Powerhouse Arts in Brooklyn, animal welfare scientist Dr. Holly Molinaro observed dogs from The Sato Project as they explored different artworks. The dogs first had time to sniff around and become comfortable in the unfamiliar space. Their responses were then observed, including whether they looked at, sniffed, or moved away from particular pieces, or chose to lie down nearby.

    Rudolph, for example, chose to lie down in front of some sculptures but ignored others. These observations helped shape profiles associating the dogs with artistic styles such as Surrealism, Minimalism, Figurative art, and Abstraction.

    According to recent reports, the concept is playful, but its purpose is practical. A standard adoption photograph may show what a dog looks like; a creative profile offers another reason to stop scrolling and learn more about the animal behind the image.

    Someone might come for the art and leave wanting a dog. Turns out, the best thing in the gallery might have four legs and be up for adoption.

    Sources indicate that dogs respond to the world as individuals. One may eagerly approach a stranger, while another prefers to observe from a safe distance. Neither reaction alone defines the dogâs personality or tells us what kind of companion they might become with time and appropriate support.

    The Rescue Collection offers a different starting point. Instead of focusing on what is known about a dogâs past, it invites people to become curious about the dog in front of them. That first spark of interest can matter, especially for dogs who might otherwise be overlooked.

    Dogs explore their surroundings through several senses, and their behavior around unfamiliar objects can offer clues about what attracts their attention. But interpreting those responses requires care.

    Recent findings suggest that dogs also see color differently from humans. People typically have three types of color-sensitive cone cells in their retinas, while dogs have two, a form of vision known as dichromacy. Dogs distinguish blues and yellows relatively well but have more difficulty differentiating reds and greens. Their visual experience of the world is therefore different from ours.

    That doesnât mean dogs see the world in black and white. Color is only one possible influence on how they respond to an object. Shape, contrast, texture, scent, movement, and the surrounding environment may also play a part.

    In a recent development, nor does spending longer near a sculpture necessarily mean a dog prefers its artistic style. The dog may be interested in its shape or position, or simply feel comfortable resting there.

    It has been revealed that A sculpture might have us admiring its color and form. The dog? They might be more interested in giving it a sniff. Different critics, different criteria.

    Although the profiles are not scientific personality assessments or guarantees of compatibility, they do invite us to learn more about each dog. Conversations with the rescue team and time spent meeting the dog remain essential to finding a suitable match.

    Rescue work involves far more than finding adopters. Veterinary care, foster placements, transportation, behavioral support, and follow-up all require time and resources. Helping the public connect with the dogs is only one part of that work, but an crucial one.

    According to recent reports, the Sato Projectâs adoption and foster manager, Alessandra Migliore, said the organization was excited to explore fresh ways of showcasing its dogsâ personalities. The campaign is part of the organizationâs broader work to help dogs rescued in Puerto Rico find homes in the northeastern United States.

    Better a Bald Head Than a Cat That’s Dead: This Common Hair Growth Formula Is Killing Pets

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1500 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Catster

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that catster is reader-supported.
    • Humans have a rather complex and contradictory relationship with their hair.
    • In a recent development, anyone who shares a home with a cat knows that personal space is more of a suggestion than a household rule.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

    Humans have a rather complex and contradictory relationship with their hair. Many of us willingly put ourselves through torturous procedures to remove it from our legs, armpits, and just about anywhere else, while, at the same time, the quest to keep a full and lustrous head of hair fuels a billion-dollar hair growth industry. Since the 1980s, a chemical called Minoxidil has become increasingly popular as both a topical and oral treatment for baldness, but what few people realize is that the very product promising hair growth poses a serious risk to their pets. The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) is warning consumers about minoxidil toxicity in cats and dogs, highlighting a danger that deserves considerably more attention.

    In a recent development, anyone who shares a home with a cat knows that personal space is more of a suggestion than a household rule. Cats rub against our heads, groom our hair, curl up on our pillows, and somehow manage to investigate just about everything we touch. These perfectly normal feline behaviors can turn deadly when minoxidil enters the picture.

    The history of minoxidil shares similarities with another well-known human drug: Viagra, which essentially took a common side effect of the heart medication, sildenafil, and turned it into its primary purpose. In the 1970s, researchers developing a newly introduced blood pressure medication found that a common side effect of the drug, minoxidil, was hypertrichosis, aka excessive hair growth. Like the story of sildenafil, the makers of minoxidil leaned into this side effect, repurposing the drug as a treatment for hair loss.1.

    In a recent development, in 1988, the FDA officially approved minoxidil, and it quickly gained popularity in products like Rogaine. Minoxidil works by widening blood vessels, a process called vasodilation, and altering the hair growth cycle to stimulate hair growth. But what helps us fight hair loss can be dangerous for our feline roommates.

    A 2021 study published in the Journal of the American Animal Hospital Association examined 211 reported cases of topical minoxidil exposure in dogs and cats. Of the 87 animals that developed signs of poisoning, 62 were cats, and 25 were dogs. Eight cats died. A 2025 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology identified another 94 reported cases, including 68 cats, ten of which died. Notably, 55 of 57 cases involving accidental exposure to a person's minoxidil treatment involved cats.

    How does this happen? Topical minoxidil is applied directly to the scalp, either as a liquid using a dropper or as a foam spread with the fingers. Medication can remain on the hands, hair, or nearby surfaces. Cats don't need to break into the medicine cabinet; a little grooming, an affectionate head rub, or a snooze on a contaminated pillow may be enough to expose them. Some were even exposed through everyday contact with their follicle-challenged cat parents.

    Recent findings suggest that minoxidil works by relaxing blood vessels and improving blood flow. In cats, however, the effects can become dangerously disruptive.

    According to recent reports, when absorbed, it can cause blood pressure to drop dramatically, a condition called hypotension. To compensate, the heart beats faster, but this doesn't necessarily solve the problem. Serious complications can follow, including fluid accumulation in the lungs (pulmonary edema) or in the space surrounding them (pleural effusion). Breathing becomes increasingly difficult, and severe poisoning can progress to cardiovascular and respiratory failure.

    Now, what should you look out for? You might notice unusual tiredness, weakness, vomiting, or a sudden loss of appetite. More concerningly, your kitty may start breathing faster than usual or appear to struggle for air. And here's the tricky part: some cats may initially seem perfectly fine.

    That's why a suspected exposure should never be brushed off simply because your cat appears normal. Waiting for visible signs of poisoning can waste valuable time.

    Now that we are beginning to appreciate the risks this product poses to our pets, we have to wonder how many unexplained cat and dog deaths could be attributed to unknown minoxidil exposure.

    Rapunzel may have had a tower to keep her hair safe, but cat owners need a different strategy: keeping minoxidil well away from curious paws.

    It has been revealed that if you use topical minoxidil, make sure you apply it in a room your cat cannot access. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water immediately afterward, and clean up any spills promptly. Used tissues, cotton pads, applicators, and empty containers should go straight into a secure bin. That tissue you casually leave on the bathroom counter? To your cat, it might look like just another interesting thing to investigate.

    It has been revealed that and what about bedtime? If you apply minoxidil in your bedroom, make closing the door part of your nighttime routine. Your cat may protest being left out of the bedroom, especially if your pillow is their favorite sleeping spot, but keeping them away from treated hair, skin, pillows, and bedding can help prevent accidental contact with medication residue. Remember, allowing the product to dry does not guarantee that every surface is free from contamination.

    You might be wondering whether switching to oral minoxidil would solve the problem. Unfortunately, not entirely. Oral minoxidil is also toxic to cats if they accidentally ingest a tablet. Whichever formulation you use, keep the medication securely stored and well out of paws' reach. Or better yet, look into options that donât put your pet at risk.

    Sources indicate that discuss your household's furry residents with the prescribing dermatologist and establish a routine that prevents accidental exposure. Cats are wonderfully persistent creatures. They may not appreciate a closed door or understand why their favorite pillow is suddenly off-limits, but a little inconvenience is a small price to pay for keeping them safe.

    If your cat licks minoxidil, contacts a spill, or may have groomed contaminated fur, contact your veterinarian or an animal poison control service immediately, even if your kitty seems perfectly fine.

    Treatment depends on the exposure and your cat's condition. It may involve hospitalization, cardiovascular monitoring, oxygen therapy, intravenous support, and medications to manage complications such as low blood pressure or fluid accumulation.

    It has been revealed that never attempt to induce vomiting or administer home remedies unless specifically instructed by a veterinary professional. If medication is still on your cat's coat or skin, ask your veterinarian how to handle decontamination safely rather than delaying emergency care.

    Unfortunately, not every cat survives minoxidil poisoning, making every accidental exposure a veterinary emergency.

    hhttps://www.instagram.com/reel/DeF7upKOC-1/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&dmpr=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==.

    Hair loss can affect confidence, and wanting to treat it is perfectly understandable. Minoxidil can be a valuable treatment for people experiencing certain types of hair loss, but sharing a home with a cat adds an crucial responsibility.

    In a recent development, preventing accidental poisoning starts with awareness. As pet parents, we need to be mindful of the products we bring into our homes, even those that seem perfectly harmless to us. From seemingly innocent houseplants and everyday foods to cleaning products, medications, and personal care treatments, many things we use routinely can pose risks to our feline companions. Before introducing something new into your home, take a moment to consider whether it is safe for your cat. A little research and a few precautions can make a world of difference.

    Industry observers note that cats will continue doing what cats do best: following their humans, investigating everything, claiming the pillows, and showing affection on their own terms. We cannot expect them to understand why a particular patch of skin or a freshly treated pillow is suddenly off-limits. That responsibility belongs to us.

    Sources indicate that thinning hair can be frustrating, even damaging to self-esteem, but itâs not a life-threatening condition. Losing a beloved pet to an avoidable medication exposure is a tragedy no one should have to experience.

    According to recent reports, better bald than catless. Every single time.

    For years, business owners and property managers have wrestled with the same question: how do you tell the difference between a legitimate service animal and a pet that someone is trying to pass off as one?

    Itâs a question John Bradford spent years trying to answer, first as a property manager overseeing thousands of rental units, and now as the founder of PetScreening, a platform used to verify animal accommodation requests across more than 7 million rental units nationwide.

    With the rising number of service dogs and emotional support animals leading to incidents of confusion, conflict, and exploitation, John sets the record straight on how to verify a real service animal from one that isn't, and what you are legally allowed to ask.

    According to recent reports, the truth is that most people donât fully understand the laws around service animals and emotional support animals, and even well-meaning questions can come across as anything but. That gray area and confusion can create real risk. Ask the wrong question, and a business can face a discrimination complaint. Ask no questions at all, and policies and rules become easy to bend, which leads to potentially dangerous situations.

    Getting this right protects everyone involved, including the people who genuinely rely on these animals every day.

    Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), service animals are defined as:.

    âDogs that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for people with disabilities.â.

    Disabilities vary widely, from physical and sensory to psychiatric, intellectual, and neurological. The needs of each person are different, so the trained tasks may look different from person to person. The ADA cites that the service animal must be a dog or, in rare cases, a miniature horse. Federal law does not require certifications, registrations, vests, or ID cards for these animals.

    In a recent development, beyond the specification that the animal must be trained to perform tasks, the legal standard is limited, so it can be difficult to easily identify which animals are legitimately service dogs and which are not. This is where public confusion starts.

    There are plenty of ways to make a dog look like a service animal, like labeled vests, âregistrationâ certifications, and IDs, but none of these are federally supported. A dog wearing a vest isnât automatically a service animal, and a dog without one isnât automatically a pet. What matters legally is not appearance or paperwork. Itâs the dogâs trained ability to perform certain tasks.

    According to recent reports, this is the distinction many find hardest to grasp, and it matters because different laws apply to each. Service dogs are protected under the ADA and, due to their training and the tasks they perform, they are permitted in public spaces such as restaurants, retail stores, and hotels. That could mean guiding someone who is visually impaired, alerting an owner to an oncoming seizure, or reminding them to take medication. Service animals are also protected under the Fair Housing Act and require paperwork if the disability or need for the animal is not obviously understood.

    In a recent development, emotional support animals (ESAs) are different. Their value comes from the comfort their presence provides. They donât necessarily have to be dogs, they arenât required to be trained to perform specific tasks, and theyâre not covered by the ADA to be allowed in public spaces like restaurants.

    They are, however, protected by the Fair Housing Act. Under this, landlords are generally required to make allowances for an ESA if a tenant has appropriate documentation from a licensed healthcare provider establishing a disability-related need. Examples of disabilities warranting an ESA include, but are not limited to, anxiety disorders or autism.

    It has been revealed that ESA accommodations are supposed to come through legitimate means, typically an established relationship with a licensed medical or mental health professional who can document the need. But some people have found loopholes for this by filling out forms online or paying fees for instant letters, which only fuels public skepticism about the legitimate need for these animals. Not to mention, this abuse can make people wary of service dogs, too.

    Industry observers note that while there is no foolproof visual test, trained service animals typically display consistent, recognizable behaviors. These dogs show exemplary discipline and obedience to the commands of their handler. They have the ability to ignore external distractions from other dogs, people, food, sounds, and smells while focusing on the needs of their handler. They display a calm temperament and are not aggressive or anxious. It is also expected that these animals be quiet, unless they are tasked with alerting an owner to a medical glitch, and that they are housebroken and trained to walk on a leash without unnecessary pulling or circling.

    This is where business owners and landlords need to tread carefully. When it isnât obvious that a dog is a service animal, staff are permitted to ask:.

    Is this dog required because of a disability?

    What task has it been trained to perform?

    Thatâs the full extent of it. Staff should not ask about the nature of a personâs disability, demand documentation or proof of training, or require dogs to demonstrate their tasks. Asking beyond the two questions, even if it comes from a place of genuine curiosity or caution, can expose a business to discrimination claims.

    Industry observers note that news stories about supposed service animals harming bystanders in public continue to raise questions about the legitimacy of those animals, and businesses are often caught in the crossfire. These incidents are symptoms of a larger problem: businesses and property owners navigating without clear guidance, while people with legitimate needs are met with suspicion.

    Service animals and emotional support animals play an essential role in the lives of the people who rely on them, and protecting that role starts with understanding the rules.

    Industry observers note that if you own a business or manage a property, you donât need to become legal experts overnight, but you do need a consistent, fair process that respects peopleâs rights and keeps everyone safe. When everyone knows where the lines are, the people who truly depend on these animals can go about their lives without facing doubt at every door.

    Tech Report: Turkey and Gravy and Pumpkin - Oh My! What Cats Can and Can’t Eat at Thanksgiving

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Catster

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

    Cats are famously persistent beggars, and a holiday table full of tempting smells gives them plenty of motivation. Although there are a handful of Thanksgiving dishes that are fine in small amounts, several can make a cat seriously ill, so it pays to know which is which before anything gets shared.

    The following foods are generally harmless for cats, provided the portions stay small and there are no pre-existing health complications. Of course, safe doesnât always mean healthy, and moderation is key. Just like people, cats also differ in what they like, and many will show no interest in some of these at all.

    Industry observers note that plain turkey is the best choice, since cats are obligate carnivores and tend to love it. It needs to be free of skin, fat, bones, gravy, and spices, and a small piece is plenty. The best thing to do is set aside a small amount to cook without all the frills, rather than cleaning it later.

    According to recent reports, plain, cooked pumpkin is non-toxic and good for a catâs digestion, and it may even soothe an upset stomach. A puree or mash works well. Pumpkin pie is a different matter, because the sugar and possible dairy arenât good for cats.

    Industry observers note that apples are safe and offer vitamins C and K, calcium, and fiber. The seeds, leaves, and stems contain cyanide and must be removed, and the fruit should be chopped into small cubes.

    In a recent development, plain green beans, minus butter, spices, herbs, onion, or garlic, are a good source of fiber and can even stand in for regular treats. Broccoli is also safe if it is unseasoned and boiled or steamed. Itâs unlikely a cat will want it, but it provides antioxidants and supports digestion. As with any new food, itâs best to introduce it carefully. Cranberry sauce isnât toxic, but its sugar content makes it unhealthy, so only an incredibly small taste is appropriate.

    Some Thanksgiving staples should never be shared, because they can make a cat quite ill.

    In a recent development, garlic, onions, leeks, scallions, and similar vegetables can be deadly even in small amounts, and garlic powder is particularly problematic. They damage a catâs red blood cells and lead to anemia, with signs such as weakness, a high heart rate, diarrhea, vomiting, and collapse. Cats are more sensitive to them than dogs, and symptoms have reportedly appeared after less than a teaspoon of cooked onion.

    Many stuffings contain onions or garlic. Even without them, stuffing is usually rich with ingredients like turkey grease that can upset a catâs stomach. It wonât be deadly without those ingredients, but it has no nutritional value and can wreak havoc on digestion.

    Sources indicate that bones should stay well out of reach. Cooked bones in particular can splinter or crack and could tear the mouth, break teeth, cause choking, or block the digestive system, and bacteria are a concern too. Keep them well out of reach.

    Recent findings suggest that chocolate is incredibly toxic to cats, and the darker it is, the worse it gets. The theobromine and caffeine it contains can cause vomiting, muscle tremors, diarrhea, an abnormal heart rate, and seizures, and it can even lead to death. Anything else with caffeine, including coffee, is off limits as well.

    According to recent reports, grapes and raisins can lead to kidney failure, and even a tiny amount of either, or related dried fruits like craisins, can cause illness. Signs include continuous vomiting, stomach distress, and hyperactivity. Some cats show no symptoms after eating them, but that isnât a reason to take the chance.

    It has been revealed that gravy isnât toxic, but it is salty and fatty, which cats donât need much of. Those levels could cause further problems for a cat with heart trouble. A sneaky lick is nothing to worry about, but gravy shouldnât be mixed into a catâs food.

    According to recent reports, A bowl of milk may seem harmless, but many cats are lactose intolerant. Dairy can give them a stomach ache, gas, or diarrhea, so itâs better to offer something from the safe list instead if theyâre sniffing around the kitchen.

    Industry observers note that raw meat and fish can carry pathogens such as E. coli and Salmonella that make cats ill, so avoid the temptation to drop some scraps as youâre preparing meals.

    A cat can share in the holiday with a nibble of plain turkey or a spoonful of pumpkin, but a few ordinary ingredients you may have around the table can cause illness and even death. With a little care over what goes into the bowl, both cat and family can enjoy a safe and happy Thanksgiving.

    In a recent development, my dog, Reggie, has Cherry eye. If left untreated, can it have a negative effect on his vision? Money is an concern for me right now.â.

    Cherry eye happens when the gland of the third eyelid, which helps produce tears, slips out of its normal position and becomes visible as a pink or red cherry-looking bulge in the corner of your dog's eye. I understand that veterinary expenses can be difficult to manage, and it is key to know what needs attention right away and what can safely wait a bit longer.

    Cherry eye does not usually cause blindness directly, but leaving it untreated can put Reggie's eye health at risk. The exposed gland can become irritated, inflamed, or damaged, and its tear production may be reduced over time. Because this gland contributes to keeping the eye moist and protected, reduced tear production can increase the risk of dry eye, a condition that can lead to corneal damage, scarring, and impaired vision if it becomes severe. Think of the gland as part of the eye's built-in lubrication system. Even if the eye looks comfortable today, problems can develop gradually.

    If surgery is not financially possible right now, please arrange a veterinary examination to confirm the diagnosis, assess tear production, and check the cornea.

    Talk to your vet about a payment strategy, or you might be able to find a veterinary teaching hospital or nonprofit clinic that may offer lower-cost care. Your veterinarian may recommend a suitable lubricating eye product while you work toward surgery, but lubrication will not reposition the gland. Please make sure you avoid human eye drops, leftover medications, or steroid eye drops unless specifically prescribed, as some of these can worsen an undiagnosed corneal ulcer. The gland should generally be repositioned and preserved rather than removed. If the gland is removed, you would need to use eye drops to supplement Reggieâs tear production for the rest of his life.

    Please seek same-day veterinary care if you see Reggie squinting, holding the eye closed, rubbing it persistently, developing a cloudy or bluish cornea, or producing thick yellow or green discharge. These can be signs of a painful or more serious eye problem. If the eye is comfortable and clear, it may not be an immediate emergency, but I would not leave cherry eye unassessed for weeks or months. The most notable first step is protecting the eye while finding an affordable treatment option.

    What Your Cat Can Teach You About Aging Well

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Catster

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that catster is reader-supported.
    • How to recognize the subtle difference between normal aging and cognitive decline, and help your senior cat stay engaged, comfortable, and independent.
    • It has been revealed that she may take a little longer to rise from her favorite chair.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

    How to recognize the subtle difference between normal aging and cognitive decline, and help your senior cat stay engaged, comfortable, and independent.

    Watch a healthy older cat move through her day.

    It has been revealed that she may take a little longer to rise from her favorite chair. She may think twice before jumping onto a countertop she once reached without hesitation. She sleeps more, chooses her routines carefully, and has become remarkably skilled at persuading the people around her to bring things closer.

    But she is still interested in breakfast. She still appears when a favorite person enters the room. She watches birds through the window, investigates a new cardboard box, and may still insist that 4:57 a.m. is a perfectly reasonable time to discuss breakfast.

    The difference matters, and I learned that the hard way with my own cat.

    Houdini was an eighteen-year-old black long-haired male who had never given me reason to worry. Then he started calling out at night, insistent enough that I could not ignore it. It would have been easy to write off as just aging. Old cats do that.

    According to recent reports, I ran a full workup instead. It showed kidney values just slightly above normal and nothing else. Apart from the calling, he still seemed to be enjoying his life. Between the pattern of the vocalizing and a workup that ruled out anything else driving it, the diagnosis was feline cognitive dysfunction.

    I lost Houdini to kidney failure about six months later.

    According to recent reports, his story is a small, real version of the point this whole article is making. The calling was not eccentricity, and it was not only age. It was cognitive change, arriving quietly, in a cat who by almost every other measure still seemed like himself.

    Scientists increasingly distinguish between two ideas: lifespan, how long we live, and healthspan, the years we remain healthy, active, independent, and engaged with life.

    It is a concept that applies beautifully to cats.

    Industry observers note that for a cat, aging well means more than reaching 15, 17, or even 20. It means continuing to move comfortably, use the litter box, groom, sleep peacefully, interact with family, explore familiar surroundings, and remain interested in the world.

    And sometimes, the first sign that something is changing is not found in a laboratory.

    Cats are remarkably good at making gradual change difficult to notice.

    In a recent development, A dog that suddenly struggles to climb the stairs tends to make the problem obvious. A cat simply stops going upstairs. The favorite sleeping place moves from the top of the bookcase to the sofa. The cat who once greeted you at the door is always asleep when you come home.

    Industry observers note that the litter-box accident is blamed on stubbornness. The midnight crying is dismissed as eccentricity. The cat who no longer jumps onto the bed is just getting old.

    Some slowing is expected with age. But newly introduced or progressive changes should not automatically be dismissed as a normal part of aging.

    Jump less often or choose lower resting places.

    Take longer to move after resting.

    Need easier access to food, water, litter boxes, or favorite furniture.

    Changes to discuss with your veterinarian.

    Seem lost or confused in familiar rooms.

    Stare at walls or hesitate at familiar doorways.

    Wander or vocalize repeatedly at night.

    Sleep much of the day but become restless after dark.

    Become unusually withdrawn, clingy, anxious, or irritable.

    Begin eliminating outside the litter box.

    Show a marked decline in activity or interest.

    Struggle to reach familiar places.

    Changes in memory, awareness, sleep, and behavior can occur with feline cognitive dysfunction, the feline counterpart of age-related dementia, but they may also be caused by pain or illness.[1].

    Sources indicate that arthritis can make a cat stop jumping. Kidney disease, diabetes, or thyroid disease can change drinking, urination, activity, and sleep. High blood pressure can affect vision and behavior. Pain, hearing loss, and declining eyesight can all make an older cat behave differently.[2].

    That is why "sheâs just getting old" can be one of the most misleading explanations in senior-cat care. Old age itself is not a disease. Sometimes a subtle behavioral change is the first clue that something treatable is happening.

    How she asks for food and whether she greets you at the door.

    Which chair she prefers and how often she plays.

    Whether she has always talked at night, or only started recently.

    It has been revealed that those ordinary observations are valuable because many age-related changes happen gradually. Once a month, stop and consciously look at your cat as though you had not seen her for several weeks.

    Is she still jumping to the same places?

    Do her back or hindquarters look thinner?

    Is she sleeping at the same times?

    Has nighttime activity or vocalization changed?

    Is she using the litter box reliably?

    Does she still interact with people and other pets in the same way?

    Does she ever seem confused in familiar places?

    Is she still interested in food, play, windows, smells, and everyday family activity?

    Look for change from your catâs own normal. A 17-year-old cat who has always slept most of the day is very different from a 12-year-old whose sleep pattern suddenly changes.

    Your cat is her own best comparison.

    Owners cannot observe their cats 24 hours a day. A few simple tools can help fill in the gaps.

    Some owners use a cat-friendly wearable activity monitor to track movement and rest over time. The value is never one isolated number. It is the pattern, and whether that pattern is shifting from the catâs own normal.

    It has been revealed that the simplest tool is your phone. Every few months, record your cat walking, jumping, climbing stairs, playing, or interacting with you. A video from six months ago often reveals gradual change that memory alone smooths over. Senior-cat care guidelines specifically encourage tracking mobility and behavior at home, because subtle changes are otherwise easy to miss.[2].

    One of the most useful discoveries about feline aging concerns something owners can actually see and feel: muscle.

    Researchers who repeatedly examined 209 pet cats, some for as long as seven years, found that muscle condition often began declining between about 7 and 10 years of age and deteriorated more rapidly as cats became older.[3].

    Body weight did not always fall at the same time.

    It has been revealed that that means a cat can appear to maintain roughly the same number on the scale while quietly losing muscle. Muscle that helps an older cat stand, balance, jump, climb into the litter box, groom, and remain independent.

    Look along the spine, shoulders, hips, and hind legs.

    Does she hesitate before jumping?

    Does she pull herself onto furniture with her front legs instead of springing upward?

    Has she stopped visiting favorite places because they are harder to reach?

    These changes deserve attention even when body weight seems stable.

    Aging well is not simply about surviving another birthday. It is about preserving the ability to do things.

    Cats teach another useful lesson about aging: Independence sometimes depends on accepting help.

    A cat who no longer jumps onto the bed may still want to sleep beside you. A small step or ramp can restore that choice.

    A cat with painful joints may stop using a litter box not because she has forgotten her training, but because climbing over the side hurts.

    A cat who becomes confused at night may do better when furniture stays in familiar places, and the path between sleeping areas, water, food, and litter boxes is simple and predictable.

    Food and water that are easy to reach.

    Steps or ramps to favorite furniture.

    Warm, supportive sleeping areas.

    Rugs or runners on slippery floors.

    Consistent placement of notable resources.

    Easy access to windows, scents, toys, and other forms of stimulation.

    Regular social contact, on the catâs terms.

    According to recent reports, the goal is not to make an old cat behave like a young cat. It is to help an old cat do the things that make her life her own.

    It has been revealed that the science behind feline aging has become especially interesting in the past few years. A 2026 study comparing thousands of observations across cats, humans, and other mammals found that cat and human brains age in strikingly similar ways, estimating that a 15-year-old cat is at roughly the same stage of brain aging as an 80-year-old person.[5] That is not a simple cat-years-to-human-years formula, but it does suggest cats experience brain aging in ways surprisingly relevant to us.

    Scientists have also found deposits of amyloid-beta, the protein associated with Alzheimerâs disease in people, in the brains of cats that had shown signs of cognitive dysfunction.[6] Cats are not tiny humans, but the overlap is strong enough that naturally aging cats may help researchers understand how brains age in both species.

    Recent findings suggest that none of this points to a single cause or a single fix. Muscle, movement, sleep, pain, metabolism, kidney function, and brain health all seem to influence each other in aging cats,[7] which is why healthy aging rarely comes from one supplement or treatment. It is a whole-animal process.

    A major 2024 study examining nearly 8,000 cat deaths in the United Kingdom estimated average life expectancy at birth at about 11.7 years, although females lived somewhat longer than males and mixed-breed cats lived longer than purebred cats as groups.[8].

    But averages do not predict the future of one individual cat.

    One encouraging finding was that a cat who had already reached 15 still had, on average, about 2.7 additional years of expected life in that population.[8].

    A 15th birthday does not necessarily mean the end is near.

    How can we make the years ahead good ones?

    There is something wonderfully symmetrical about all of this.

    We are beginning to study cats because they may help us understand how brains and bodies age, and at the same time, they may already be teaching us the larger lesson.

    Aging well may not mean remaining unchanged. It may mean adapting while preserving what matters:.

    And the desire to remain engaged with the world.

    There may even be a benefit flowing in the other direction.

    Recent findings suggest that A 2025 study found that cat and dog owners indicated a slower decline in some measures of memory and thinking than people who did not own pets. Among cat owners, the association included verbal ability and delayed memory.[9].

    The study cannot prove that cats caused the difference, but it offers a delightful possibility:.

    While we study our cats to understand healthy aging, sharing our lives with them may also be connected with aspects of healthier aging in us.

    That is part of why my colleagues and I at Veterinary Health Research Centers developed CATMA, Cats Advancing Toward Mindful Aging, to help owners and veterinarians recognize meaningful change earlier.

    Not simply more years. More good years.

    The next time you see your older cat asleep in a patch of sunlight, consider what she may be telling you.

    She knows whether she can reach her favorite chair.

    Whether the house feels familiar.

    Whether her legs carry her where she wants to go.

    Whether there are still interesting things to investigate.

    Whether someone she trusts is nearby.

    Perhaps that is as good a definition of aging well as any of us has found.

    Is Your Dog Weird Enough for Times Square?

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
